items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications Across the Perioperative Continuum of Adult Cardiovascular Surgery: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Cardiovascular surgery generates a large volume of physiological, hemodynamic, and imaging data across the perioperative continuum, which has favored the accelerated incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) tools—including machine learning, deep learning, neural networks, computer vision, natural language processing, and, more recently, generative AI models based on large language models—into virtually every phase of perioperative care. Recent literature documents a rapid increase in AI-related publications in cardiac surgery since 2020, spanning surgical risk stratification, structural intervention planning, automated interpretation of cardiovascular imaging, intraoperative monitoring, cardiopulmonary bypass optimization, and prediction of postoperative complications such as acute kidney injury, low cardiac output syndrome, delirium, atrial fibrillation, and respiratory failure, as well as emerging applications in telemedicine and remote follow-up. However, existing evidence remains fragmented across reviews focused on isolated perioperative phases or single complications, and no scoping review to date has comprehensively mapped AI applications across the entire perioperative continuum. This protocol describes a scoping review, conducted following the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and reported according to PRISMA-ScR guidelines, aiming to map and characterize the available evidence on AI applications throughout the perioperative process of adult cardiovascular surgery. The Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework will guide eligibility criteria. Searches will be conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library, complemented by grey literature, with publications from 2010 onward. Two independent reviewers will conduct study selection and data extraction using a standardized JBI-based charting form. Findings will be synthesized descriptively and presented through evidence tables, an AI technology taxonomy, a classification by perioperative phase and clinical purpose, and a conceptual map, identifying key knowledge gaps to guide future research.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Anesthesiology and Intensive Care Medicine: Current Evidence, Clinical Readiness and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated across anesthesiology and intensive care medicine (ICM), where complex data, continuous monitoring, and time-sensitive decisions create substantial opportunities for computational decision support. However, the clinical readiness of many AI applications remains uncertain. Methods: This narrative review provides a structured and clinically oriented synthesis of AI applications in anesthesiology and ICM. PubMed and Google Scholar were searched for English-language publications from January 2019 to December 2025 using the terms “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “deep learning,” “large language models,” “ChatGPT,” “anesthesiology,” “anesthesia,” “perioperative,” “intensive care,” and “critical care.” Studies with direct or potential clinical relevance to perioperative or intensive care practice were considered, and the selected literature was synthesized descriptively. Results: Forty-seven publications were included, encompassing systematic reviews and meta-analyses, narrative and scoping reviews, retrospective and prospective studies, randomized trials, and model development, validation, and evaluation studies. In anesthesiology, AI applications included preoperative risk stratification, difficult airway assessment, hemodynamic monitoring, closed-loop anesthesia, ultrasound-assisted procedures, postoperative outcome prediction, and perioperative communication. In ICM, major applications involved mortality and sepsis risk assessment, respiratory failure and mechanical ventilation management, intelligent alarm systems, delirium detection, sedation monitoring, and large language model (LLM)-assisted documentation. Although several approaches demonstrated promising predictive or supportive capabilities, prospective and randomized evidence remained limited. External validation, real-world clinical evaluation, data quality, model transparency, privacy, accountability, and regulatory uncertainty were recurring challenges. Conclusion: AI technologies have substantial potential to support clinical decision-making, situational awareness, individualized care, and workflow efficiency in anesthesiology and ICM. However, most applications remain in early stages of clinical translation. Current evidence supports their use as complementary, clinician-supervised tools rather than autonomous decision-makers. Robust prospective validation, standardized evaluation, ethical governance, and alignment with clinical needs are essential for safe and meaningful integration into routine practice.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Driven Business Innovation and AI Governance A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed modern business environments by enhancing operational efficiency, supporting data-driven decision-making, and enabling the development of innovative business models. However, the widespread adoption of AI also introduces governance-related challenges, including issues of transparency, accountability, ethics, privacy, and regulatory compliance, making AI governance an increasingly important area of concern. This study aims to systematically review the existing literature on AI-driven business innovation and AI governance to identify current research trends, major themes, opportunities, and challenges in the field. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) methodology was employed by collecting and analyzing relevant scholarly articles from major academic databases based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The results reveal that AI contributes substantially to business innovation through process automation, predictive analytics, enhanced customer engagement, and strategic decision-making, while effective AI governance frameworks facilitate responsible AI adoption, strengthen stakeholder trust, and support sustainable digital transformation. The review further highlights that organizations achieving a balance between technological innovation and governance practices are better positioned to maximize the benefits of AI while mitigating potential risks. In conclusion, AI-driven business innovation and AI governance are mutually reinforcing factors that play a critical role in promoting sustainable business growth and long-term organizational competitiveness in the digital era.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for early detection and prevention of ventilator-induced lung injury: a scoping review
items.abstract: Abstract Background The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into intensive care unit (ICU) ventilator management has attracted growing research interest, with studies exploring applications ranging from surveillance and decision support toward more autonomous ventilatory adjustment. Whether this represents a clinically validated transition from reactive to proactive ventilation management remains to be established through prospective evidence. This review maps the available literature on these developments in the context of ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI), a heterogeneous syndrome including barotrauma, volutrauma, atelectrauma, and biotrauma. This review maps AI applications relevant to VILI detection and prevention, rather than studies that directly demonstrate VILI prevention. Methods This scoping review mapped and synthesized evidence on the use of AI-based systems for the early detection and prevention of VILI in critically ill adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. Following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines, a systematic search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and the Biblioteca Virtual en Salud (BVS) for literature published between 2010 and 2026. Results A total of 52 studies met full-text inclusion criteria. Most AI applications focused on automated detection of patient-ventilator asynchronies, prediction of complications related to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and optimization of lung-protective ventilation parameters through machine learning and reinforcement learning approaches. Although AI-based systems may support more individualized ventilatory management strategies, their clinical implementation remains limited by the lack of external validation, methodological heterogeneity, and scarce evidence in low- and middle-income settings. Conclusions The evidence identified is predominantly technical, retrospective and exploratory, and rests largely on surrogate physiological or classification endpoints. High diagnostic accuracy, or improvement in surrogate parameters, does not by itself constitute evidence that these systems prevent VILI or improve patient-centred outcomes. Current evidence therefore supports the promise of these applications and the prioritization of prospective research, but not their routine clinical implementation.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in Acute Care Surgery: integrating new capabilities into a complex adaptive system
items.abstract: Acute Care Surgery (ACS) emerged not as a single innovation, but as the progressive integration of operative discipline, intensive care, trauma systems, biologically informed resuscitation, and regionalized care infrastructure into a layered, complex, adaptive system. Artificial intelligence (AI) now represents the next major technological layer being introduced into this mature sociotechnical environment. This narrative review examines ACS from a systems perspective and argues that the success or failure of AI integration requires both algorithmic performance and how effectively these technologies couple with existing workflows, operational structures, feedback mechanisms, and clinical decision-making processes. Historical developments in ACS - including intensive care evolution, trauma system regionalization, damage control philosophy, and prior failures of reductionist biologic interventions - provide important lessons for understanding the opportunities and risks of AI deployment in high-acuity surgical care. Current AI applications in ACS include augmented diagnostics, continuous physiologic surveillance, predictive analytics, operative video analysis, workflow optimization, and educational assessment. However, important issues remain, including alert fatigue, automation bias, implementation failure, inequitable model generalizability, and the risks of introducing reductionist computational paradigms into complex adaptive systems. A systems-oriented framework emphasizes that AI tools must be evaluated not as isolated products, but as components of broader clinical, organizational, and educational ecosystems. ACS, with its longstanding experience integrating layered technologies and coordinating multidisciplinary care under conditions of uncertainty, may represent one of the most informative environments in which to study responsible AI implementation in surgery.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Graphic Design: Exploring Creativity and Challenges
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly become part of contemporary visual communication and is changing the way graphic designers generate, develop, refine, and present ideas. Tools based on generative AI can produce images, illustrations, layouts, typography suggestions, visual variations, and creative concepts within seconds. For graphic designers, this development offers significant opportunities for experimentation and efficiency, but it also raises important questions about creativity, originality, authorship, professional identity, and the future of design education. This paper explores the relationship between artificial intelligence and graphic design from the perspective of creative practice. The paper argues that AI does not eliminate the need for human creativity; instead, it changes where creative effort takes place. Designers increasingly need to formulate problems, evaluate generated possibilities, make cultural and aesthetic judgments, refine outputs, and give visual communication a meaningful human direction. At the same time, excessive dependence on AI may lead to design fixation, visual similarity, weakened foundational skills, and uncertainty regarding authorship. The paper concludes that the most productive future for graphic design lies in responsible human–AI collaboration, supported by strong foundations in design principles, visual thinking, ethics, and critical judgment.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Interior Design: Opportunities, Challenges and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the design industry by introducing data-driven, generative, predictive, and automated approaches to creative and technical processes. Interior design, traditionally dependent on human creativity, spatial understanding, material knowledge, and client preferences, is increasingly influenced by AI-powered tools capable of generating design concepts, visualizations, layouts, material combinations, lighting solutions, and personalized spatial recommendations. Recent developments in generative AI, machine learning, computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal systems have expanded the possibilities for designers to explore a larger number of alternatives in less time. This research paper examines the opportunities, challenges, and future perspectives associated with the integration of Artificial Intelligence into interior design. The study adopts a qualitative systematic literature review approach and synthesizes recent research on AI-assisted architectural and built-environment design. The review indicates that AI can support concept generation, space planning, 3D visualization, material selection, sustainability analysis, personalization, and client communication. However, issues related to creativity, algorithmic bias, intellectual property, data privacy, professional responsibility, design authenticity, technical skills, and overdependence on automated systems remain significant challenges. Recent systematic reviews show that AI research in design is strongly concentrated in early conceptual and schematic stages, while later stages requiring detailed technical, contextual, and professional judgment remain comparatively underexplored. The paper argues that AI should not be viewed as a replacement for interior designers but as an augmentation technology that can strengthen human creativity, decision-making, and productivity. A human-centred AI framework combining technological capability with professional expertise, ethical safeguards, cultural sensitivity, and user participation is proposed. The study concludes that the future of interior design will increasingly depend on effective human–AI collaboration rather than complete automation.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in orthopaedics should be built with surgeons, not just for them!
items.abstract: Abstract Surgical artificial intelligence (AI) is typically validated on one patient population and then deployed unchanged into another, without surgeon input into its design. AI in orthopaedics should be built with surgeons, not simply for them: Surgeons should hold shared authority over the clinical question, data curation, validation, implementation, monitoring and retirement of any tool they use. Specialty‐tuned models outperform general‐purpose systems on some tasks, but the margin is modest and likely to narrow as generalist models improve. The more durable distinction is who controls the update loop—who can retrain a model on local outcomes, audit its failures and withdraw it when it drifts. Trial evidence shows that a clinician kept in that loop by design, not as an afterthought, outperforms working alone. What determines whether orthopaedic AI fulfils its promise is not model architecture, but who stays accountable to the surgeon at the bedside when the model needs to change.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Personal Finance Management: An Empirical Study of Young Investors in the Kalyan Region
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is embedded in every financial transaction and interaction through robo-advising, auto- Recommendations, portfolios tracking, digital financial assistants, and financial information processing tools. This paper considers the relevance of AI to young investors of the Kalyan Region. Using relevant published evidence from SEBI, NSE, AMFI and RBI, along with peer-reviewed research and analysis, this paper applies descriptive, comparative and trend-oriented analysis to examine the use and impact of AI in personal finance management. Evidence shows an ageing-down of India's investor base, with young people constituting an increasing proportion of the registered individual investors. The study finds that AI can reduce information and access barriers and enable personalisation, monitoring, and analysis. However, the benefits are limited by financial literacy, trust, perceived risk, transparency and ability to question AI outputs.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Innovations in Medical Science
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence plays a crucial role today by assisting providers in patient care and supporting them in various intelligent healthcare systems. The technique shifts from computational knowledge to machine learning, which can assess complex medical data. AI is ubiquitous in Healthcare, which can be used in treatment, diagnosis, patient risk identification, and predicting the outcome of clinical scenarios. An overview of different intelligent techniques presented in this article is discussed with the receiver of clinical application, and future challenges of the current scenario of AI in Healthcare. Articles and internet searches were carried out using the keywords Artificial Intelligence and computational Healthcare. Further references were obtained from Data available on Google Scholar, PubMed, medical databases, and cross-referencing from key articles based on it. The results are also assessed using a variety of quality standards, including prediction accuracy and rate, based on the examination of several papers on disease diagnosis.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Teaching Support System for Personalized Learning in Higher Education
items.abstract: The aim of this study was to design and evaluate an artificial intelligence-driven teacher support system capable of translating multidimensional learning profiles into instructional and assessment recommendations for higher education. The proposal integrated five diagnostic dimensions: VARK, for preferences in accessing information; FSLSM, for processing and representation traits; ICAP, for levels of cognitive engagement; SRL, for self-regulated learning; and EBSI, for study habits. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods approach was used. In the quantitative phase, a digital questionnaire was administered to 145 students from five universities, and the data were processed through a system developed in Python, which generated diagnostic profiles and personalized pedagogical reports for teachers. In the qualitative phase, four instructors evaluated the usefulness, perceived coherence, feasibility, and ethical acceptability of the reports. The results showed substantial convergence between the diagnosis calculated without AI and the narrative generated with AI in dimensions such as VARK and ICAP, as well as favorable acceptance by the teaching staff. However, mismatches were identified in the calibration of FSLSM and in the intensity attributed to SRL and EBSI. It is concluded that AI can mediate instructional decision-making under pedagogical supervision

items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Accounting Ethics, and Trust in Financial Reporting: Developing an Ethical AI Governance Framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally transforming accounting practice by displacing traditional data-processing tasks, augmenting auditing functions, and reshaping the professional competency requirements of financial reporting. While these technological developments generate substantial efficiency gains, they simultaneously introduce unprecedented ethical challenges, including algorithmic opacity, accountability diffusion, bias propagation in automated judgment, and the erosion of professional scepticism — that threaten the integrity of financial reporting and the public trust upon which the accounting profession's social licence to operate ultimately depends. This paper develops a rigorous, theoretically grounded analysis of the intersection between artificial intelligence and accounting ethics, drawing on institutional theory, agency theory, virtue ethics, and the stakeholder trust framework to diagnose how AI adoption reconfigures the ethical architecture of financial reporting and to prescribe the governance, professional, and regulatory responses required to safeguard ethical standards and trust in this transformed environment. The paper makes three original contributions: first, it develops a multi-dimensional taxonomy of AI-related ethical risks in accounting, distinguishing technical, professional, and systemic risk categories; second, it proposes the Ethical AI Accounting Governance Framework (EAAGF), an original implementation model that integrates algorithmic governance, professional ethics renewal, regulatory adaptation, and stakeholder assurance mechanisms; and third, it situates these contributions within a comparative empirical analysis of AI adoption experiences across major accounting contexts, integrating evidence from surveys, regulatory reports, and case illustrations. The paper argues that the central challenge is not whether AI will transform accounting — this is already occurring — but whether the profession, regulators, and organisations can collectively construct the ethical governance infrastructure required to ensure that transformation advances rather than undermines the accountability, transparency, and trust that constitute the profession's foundational social purpose.

items.title: Autonomia w edukacji outdoorowej: Perspektywa edukatorów
items.abstract: This article explores how autonomy is understood and supported in outdoor education. The aim of the study was to examine educators’ perspectives on autonomy and its role in learning processes in outdoor settings. A qualitative research design was employed, using semi-structured interviews with 13 outdoor educators working with children and youth in the United States. The data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings indicate that autonomy in outdoor education is embodied, relational, and context-dependent. It is expressed through direct engagement with environmental challenges, opportunities for choice, and participation in group processes. Educators reported that autonomy enhances intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, and social development. Outdoor environments were found to support the integration of autonomy, competence, and relatedness, in line with Self-Determination Theory. The study highlights the importance of autonomy-supportive practices, including flexibility, trust-building, and balancing freedom with structure and safety. The results suggest that outdoor education offers a unique context for fostering autonomy as meaningful participation rather than individual independence.

items.title: Balancing the Books and the Backseat: Algorithmic Management, Student Gig Workers, and the Welfare Gap in India's AI-Driven Platform Economy under Viksit Bharat @2047
items.abstract: Abstract India's vision of Viksit Bharat @2047 rests significantly on harnessing Artificial Intelligence (AI) to power an inclusive digital economy, with the gig and platform sector projected to grow from 7.7 million workers in 2020-21 to 23.5 million by 2029-30 [1]. Within this expanding workforce lies an under-documented segment: college students who work as ride-hailing drivers and delivery partners for platforms such as Uber, Ola, Rapido, Swiggy, and Zomato alongside their academic commitments. While the Code on Social Security, 2020, operationalised through Rules notified in 2025-26, extends formal welfare recognition to gig and platform workers for the first time, it remains largely silent on the algorithmic mechanisms, dynamic pricing, rating-based deactivation, and automated task allocation, that govern their day-to-day work experience, a gap well documented in the international algorithmic-management literature [2], [3], [4]. This paper examines the intersection of AI-driven algorithmic management and worker welfare policy through a mixed-methods approach: a review of the current regulatory framework combined with primary survey data (n = 18) collected from college students in Coimbatore district engaged in gig work. The findings show that a majority of respondents report unpredictable pricing (70.6%) and roughly two in five report unfair ratings (41.2%) or deactivation/suspension (35.3%), while awareness of the e-Shram portal (52.9%) and of statutory welfare benefits (58.8%, with a further 23.5% only vaguely aware) remains partial. The paper concludes with a policy framework recommending algorithmic transparency mandates, accessible grievance redressal mechanisms, and targeted awareness measures for student and youth gig workers, contributing to the broader goal of inclusive, technology-driven, and socially secure economic growth envisioned under Viksit Bharat @2047.

items.title: Belief-Based Maximum Occupancy Principle and Active Inference
items.abstract: Intrinsic motivation plays a central role in adaptive and goal-directed behavior by conferring agents reward-independent objectives and biases useful to act in noisy and uncertain environments. Active Inference addresses the problem of acting in a partially observable environment through a principled framework for belief updating and action selection. A key component of Active Inference is the specification of prior preferences, which shapes behavior by encoding desirable future outcomes. An intrinsic motivation approach called the Maximum Occupancy Principle (MOP) proposes that agents act so as to maximize occupancy over future paths of states and actions, with no preferences or epistemic targets. Despite its simple formulation, MOP gives rise to rich and adaptive behaviors that combine exploratory variability with goal-directed dynamics. In this work, we extend MOP to partially observable environments and introduce a Bellman reformulation of the Expected Free Energy for Active Inference, both incorporating belief-based inference over hidden states as part of the agent state. The Bellman formulation enables tractable offline computation via value iteration over the full belief-state space. We compare the resulting behaviors in a set of minimal experimental settings with uncertain food sources. We find that MOP agents switch between goal-directed (food seeking) behavior and exploration between different food sources, depending on their energy available and their belief state. In contrast, Active Inference agents mostly inhabit regions around a single food source, a strategy having both high pragmatic and epistemic value. We finally compare with Empowerment, which is shown to be qualitatively similar to Active Inference.

items.title: Benchmarking the safety of large language models for robotic health attendant control
items.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for deployment as the control component of robotic health attendants (RHAs), yet their safety in this context remains poorly characterized. We introduce a dataset of 270 harmful instructions spanning nine prohibited behaviour categories grounded in the American Medical Association (AMA) Principles of Medical Ethics, and use it to evaluate 72 LLMs in a simulation environment based on the RHA framework. The mean violation rate across all models was 54.4%, with more than half exceeding 50%, and violation rates varied substantially across behaviour categories, with superficially plausible instructions such as device manipulation and emergency delay proving harder to refuse than overtly destructive ones. Model size and release date were the primary determinants of safety performance among open-weight models, and proprietary models were substantially safer than open-weight counterparts (median 23.7% versus 72.8%). Medical domain fine-tuning conferred no significant overall safety benefit, and a prompt-based defence strategy produced only a modest reduction in violation rates among the least safe models, leaving violation rates that would preclude safe clinical deployment. These findings demonstrate that safety evaluation must be treated as a first-class criterion in the development and deployment of LLM-based RHAs.

items.title: Beyond Learning Achievement: Investigating International Students’ Acceptance of Game-based Technology for Chinese Language Learning
items.abstract: While previous studies on game-based learning have primarily focused on learning achievement, achievement results alone do not explain whether learners perceive the technology as useful, easy to use, and worth continuing to use. Learner acceptance is essential because successful technology implementation depends on learners’ willingness to adopt and continue using it. This study investigated international students’ acceptance of game-based technology for Chinese language learning by integrating the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Self-Determination Theory (SDT). This acceptance-focused analysis used post-intervention questionnaire data from 40 international students enrolled in Chinese language courses at a language school in Chiang Mai, Thailand. A 12-item questionnaire measured intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, attitude, and behavioral intention. Data was analyzed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, and Pearson’s correlations. All six constructs were rated at a high level. Attitude obtained the highest mean (M = 4.18), followed by intrinsic motivation and perceived usefulness (both M = 4.16), whereas behavioral intention obtained the lowest mean (M = 4.04). Behavioral intention was positively correlated with intrinsic motivation (r = .989), extrinsic motivation (r = .980), perceived usefulness (r = .989), perceived ease of use (r = .962), and attitude (r = .988), with all relationships significant at p < .01. However, the consistently high correlations suggest possible overlap among the constructs and should be interpreted cautiously. The findings indicate that continued-use intention is closely associated with learners’ technology perceptions and motivational orientations. By focusing on students’ acceptance rather than repeating the analysis of learning achievement, this study offers practical guidance for designing useful, manageable, and engaging game-based Chinese learning environments.

items.title: Bridging the Education–Employment Gap under NEP 2020: AI Literacy, Communication Competence, and Work-Integrated Learning for Graduate Employability
items.abstract: Abstract India's expansion of higher education has created unprecedented opportunities for young people, yet the movement from educational qualification to meaningful employment remains uneven. The central challenge is no longer simply access to degrees but the relationship between credentials, capabilities, workplace experience, and employment outcomes. This conceptual paper examines how the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 can contribute to narrowing this education–employment gap through the integrated development of AI literacy, communication competence, and work-integrated learning. Drawing on recent policy evidence from NITI Aayog, the International Labour Organization, and contemporary scholarship on artificial intelligence and work-integrated learning, the paper argues that employability should not be treated as an additional soft-skills component appended to an academic curriculum. Rather, it should emerge from a coherent educational architecture connecting disciplinary knowledge with communication, digital and AI capabilities, authentic workplace exposure, critical thinking, and demonstrable competence. The paper proposes an integrated framework in which AI literacy and communication competence function as enabling capabilities, while work-integrated learning provides the context in which those capabilities are tested and developed. It concludes by suggesting institutional measures through which Indian higher education can move from credential-centred education towards competency-, experience-, and outcome-oriented graduate preparation.

items.title: Can Agents Trust Their Skills? Uncovering Unsafe Chains of Trust in Skill-Based LLM Agents
items.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on installable skills, which are packages of instructions, code, and resources that equip them with task-specific capabilities and, once installed, can be automatically invoked across subsequent user tasks. This creates a chain of trust in which users delegate authority to agents, while agent frameworks admit skill-provided content into the agents' context with insufficient validation, allowing malicious skills to influence agent behavior under that delegated authority. Yet, little is known about whether this trust model adequately constrains untrusted skill content before it reaches security-sensitive operations, or how frequently such trust violations arise in real-world agents. We present TrustProbe, a framework for uncovering unsafe chains of trust in skill-based LLM agents. First, TrustProbe analyzes agent source code to identify source-to-sink call paths from skill-controlled inputs to security-sensitive operations. Second, it generates semantically realistic SKILL.md seeds with injected canaries and evolves them through feedback-guided scheduling and mutation. Finally, it validates vulnerabilities using an oracle that confirms attacker-controlled flows and verifies observable harm. Across 11 open-source agents, eight with more than 10,000 GitHub stars, TrustProbe identifies 104 taint-style vulnerabilities. Validation on a large corpus of real-world skills collected from public hubs such as ClawHub further shows that 25.1% of skill-agent trials exercise the identified vulnerable paths, with payload injection successfully weaponizing 15 of the vulnerabilities. These results reveal a systematic trust failure in skill-based LLM agents: untrusted skill content can reach security-sensitive operations and exercise authority delegated by users to their agents.

items.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Reduce Teachers’ Workload Without Compromising Educational Interaction?
items.abstract: This study aims to examine the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) utilization as a teaching assistant on teachers’ workload and the quality of educational interactions in Islamic schools (Madrasahs). Employing a mixed-methods sequential explanatory design, the study involved 120 teachers divided into an experimental group (AI users) and a control group. Quantitative findings revealed a significant reduction in the workload of teachers using AI (Δ = -18.5 points, p < 0.001) and a significant improvement in the quality of educational interactions (Δ = +1.4 points, p < 0.001). Furthermore, a strong correlation was found between the reduction in time-related workload and the enhancement of a positive classroom climate (r = -0.72). Qualitative findings indicated that the time saved through AI assistance (16.8 hours per week) was reallocated to personal interactions with students and character development activities. The study confirms that AI has the potential to transform the teacher’s role from mu'allim (knowledge transmitter) to murabbi (character educator), provided that its implementation is managed wisely and ethically.

items.title: ChatGPT, Achievement Motivation, and Problem-Solving: Evidence from Thai and Cambodian Undergraduates
items.abstract: Background. The rapid global adoption of ChatGPT has raised growing interest in its role in supporting student learning, yet the effectiveness of generative AI tools in enhancing higher-order cognitive skills such as problem-solving may depend on individual learner characteristics that remain underexplored. Purpose. This quantitative study aimed to examine the relationship between ChatGPT usage and problem-solving ability among students enrolled in a Media Design course, and to test whether this relationship is moderated by achievement motivation. Method. The study involved 115 university students from four intact classes across two higher education institutions in Thailand and Cambodia. Data were collected through a survey questionnaire and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), preceded by a measurement invariance test (MICOM) to assess the appropriateness of pooling data across the two national samples. Results. The findings indicate that ChatGPT usage was positively and significantly associated with problem-solving ability (? = 0.386, p < 0.001), as was achievement motivation (? = 0.291, p < 0.01). The interaction between ChatGPT usage and achievement motivation also showed a significant positive effect (? = 0.157, p < 0.05), indicating that achievement motivation strengthens the relationship between ChatGPT usage and problem-solving ability. The model explained 44.6% of the variance in problem-solving ability (R² = 0.446). Conclusion. This study has significant implications for instructional practices in higher education settings, particularly for lecturers designing AI-integrated learning activities. By understanding how achievement motivation shapes students’ benefit from ChatGPT, educators can tailor instructional strategies that support both technology adoption and the development of independent problem solving skills.

items.title: Co-Creating Open Learning Materials for the Digitalisation of Energy: A Collaborative Model for Public and Expert Engagement
items.abstract: The Every1 project has developed a large, openly licensed collection of learning materials to support citizens and professionals engaging with Europe’s digitally mediated energy transitions. The project adopted an iterative methodology that combined a cyclical production pipeline, embedded co-creation, and multimodal user testing across six development cycles. Stakeholders from fourteen countries contributed through interviews, workshops, surveys, webinars and roadshow activities, generating insights that shaped both the content of the learning materials and the design process. Findings highlight the value of relational engagement, linguistic and contextual localisation, and of offering a diverse portfolio of materials to meet varied learner needs. The resulting Every1 model provides a transferable framework for co-creating open learning materials in complex sociotechnical domains. items.title: Cognitive competences in human–AI qualitative analysis: exploring the MIXAI workflow through reflective portfolios
items.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into educational research is reshaping core practices such as literature reviews and qualitative analysis. However, this methodological transition creates tension between gains in operational efficiency and the latent risk of erosion of higher-order cognitive competencies. Existing scholarship suggests that productive GenAI integration requires the deliberate exercise of these competencies to preserve the researcher's intellectual agency. Despite this, their monitoring remains underexplored. This study examines how researchers draw on three fundamental cognitive competencies (abstract, systemic, and analytical thinking) when using the MIXAI workflow in GenAI-supported methodological literature reviews. Methodologically, an embedded single case study design was adopted, with the MIXAI workflow as the instrumental case and six researchers in training as the units of analysis. The corpus of 22 reflective diary-portfolios was analyzed using the Framework Analysis Method through hybrid human–AI coding and structured cross-validation under strict human epistemic control. The results show that the five dimensions of the Abstract–Systemic–Analytical–Reflective–Integrative (ASARI) model are activated differentially: analytical thinking functions as an entry-level competence driven by workflow structure; abstract thinking is unlocked by overcoming technical barriers; and integration depends on prior disciplinary expertise. Seven emerging categories were incorporated as subdimensions, and epistemic coconstruction was identified as a frontier yet to be characterized. The productive exercise (rather than erosion) of cognitive competencies appears less dependent on technical expertise than on the presence of the regulatory dimensions, reflexivity and integration, which keep the researcher as the central epistemic authority. The model provides a framework for monitoring the conditions of GenAI collaboration, while supporting analytical rigor and the central role of human judgment in scientific knowledge production.

items.title: Coherence as a Cognitive Security Control: From Multi-Module Artificial Cognition to Human-AI Hybrid Systems
items.abstract: Executive summary Cognitive security should protect not only individual humans or individual AI models, but also the interfaces through which cognitive systems exchange representations, assumptions, memory, provenance, constraints, and decision authority. A visible AI failure is often an incorrect answer. A deeper failure can occur when every component remains locally plausible while the larger cognitive system becomes globally incoherent. In complex artificial systems, independently updated modules may remain individually functional while drifting out of alignment. In sustained Human-AI interaction, both participants may remain individually capable while their shared epistemic process progressively loses version integrity, provenance, role separation, or external validation. The security object is therefore not always a component. Sometimes the security object is the relation. Such relational failures can arise accidentally, but they can also be induced. An adversary does not need to compromise any single model, module, or person if it can degrade the relation between them. This contribution proposes coherence governance as a distinct cognitive-security control applicable to both artificial cognitive architectures and Human-AI hybrid systems. Its central rule is simple: coherence should be observable and governable, but it must never be confused with truth, agreement, confidence, or task performance.

items.title: Covert Assistance: Helpful LLM Agents Evade Oversight in Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: As multi-agent systems enter high-stakes domains, the possibility that agents may circumvent safety boundaries is a growing concern. Prior work has examined this risk primarily in adversarial settings, where agents are instructed or rewarded to communicate covertly and evade oversight. We show that benign agents can cross the same boundaries without adversarial incentives. We emulate a software-engineering workflow in which a planner represents a company hiring an external developer. The planner writes requirements and holds a company credential it is instructed not to disclose to the developer; a monitor screens their exchanges. Seven of nine tested frontier models disguise the credential in their requirements to help the developer recover it while evading the monitor, even after completing their assigned objective. For example, across 6,000 episodes with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, the planner attempts concealment in 16.9%; in 0.9%, the credential evades the monitor and is recovered and used by the developer. Despite the low per-episode rate, the risk compounds across repeated exchanges: at 0.9%, 105 independent episodes carry a 61.3% chance of at least one breach. Our analysis suggests that the planner misinterprets disguised disclosure as helping the developer and reads the nondisclosure rule as banning plaintext, not character codes or riddles. We call this behavior covert assistance. Monitoring favors concealment, while concealment gives way to direct disclosure when the recipient is presented as a human rather than an AI agent, so leakage persists. Giving the monitor the credential improves detection but requires trusting it with the secret. These risks, in models already used for software engineering, challenge oversight to distinguish authorized cooperation from task-advancing assistance that crosses safety boundaries.

items.title: CRAFT: Exploring Wearable Creative AI on Smart Glasses for Fiction Writing in Real-World Contexts
items.abstract: Creative writing increasingly integrates AI assistance, yet current tools miss in-situ moments when writers draw inspiration from real-world experiences. We envision Context-aware Reality-Fiction Transformation ( CRAFT ), an approach for AI glasses that translates daily experiences into fiction narratives. We explored its desirability, feasibility, and potential viability through three studies. Interviews with nine writers yielded desires and three design goals: 1) augmenting in-situ perception to bridge reality-fiction gaps, 2) promoting authenticity grounded in real-world experiences while maintaining fictionalization, and 3) preserving creative agency, enjoyment, and life-art boundaries. Co-design workshops with 16 writers and researchers operationalized these goals into concrete interaction mechanisms using a technology probe. We then conducted supported field trials with eight writers across 24 sessions using a refined probe, revealing writer-perceived benefits (e.g., enriched fictional ideas from serendipitous encounters), emergent practices (e.g., micro-creation), and design considerations for future sustained use. We contribute design explorations for the CRAFT approach, offering design implications and empirical insights on ubiquitous human-AI creative collaboration in everyday life.

items.title: DAIMON: Designing AI-Augmented Research Dashboards to Enable Novel Human-AI Collaborative Workflows in Longitudinal Sensing Studies
items.abstract: Researchers conduct longitudinal passive sensing studies in in-the-wild settings, often spanning months or years, to uncover naturalistic behavioral patterns. These studies are not “set-and-forget” deployments; they require continuous monitoring as technical failures and declining participant compliance can lead to substantial missing data, undermining study validity and downstream models. Thus, conducting these studies involves multiple detail-oriented, cognitively demanding, and time-consuming tasks, making it a burdensome and stressful process. Existing research dashboards, the primary tools for data monitoring, offer limited support in easing this burden. Leveraging recent advances in AI for passive sensing data, we explore the design of human-AI collaborative workflows enabled through research dashboards to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of monitoring and associated tasks. We begin with a co-design study with 13 researchers involved in longitudinal sensing studies to identify desired AI capabilities and interactions through semi-structured interviews, brainstorming, and sketching activities. We operationalize novel human-AI workflows our participants envisioned by implementing an AI-augmented dashboard prototype DAIMON , and use it as a research probe in two studies: a task-based study and a deployment within an ongoing real-world sensing study. Our findings demonstrate the promise of AI-augmented dashboards in supporting researchers' day-to-day data monitoring and decision-making tasks. It also surfaces concerns around transparency and expectations with AI systems. Consolidating insights across all three studies, we present design guidelines for AI-augmented dashboards for longitudinal passive sensing research and discuss directions for future work.

items.abstract: Electronic Health Records (EHRs) have become an essential component of healthcare digital transformation, but their implementation may also increase healthcare workers’ workload and affect their well-being. This review aimed to systematically analyze the impact of EHR implementation on healthcare workers’ workload and well-being based on recent scientific evidence. A systematic review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Literature searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Library to identify studies published between 2020 and 2025 using the PECO framework. The selection process identified 20 studies that met the predefined inclusion criteria and were subsequently synthesized using a narrative approach. The review found that EHR implementation consistently increased documentation burden, prolonged digital working hours, and elevated cognitive workload due to system complexity. Poor EHR usability was also associated with higher levels of work-related stress, burnout, emotional exhaustion, reduced job satisfaction, and impaired work–life balance among healthcare workers. The magnitude of these effects varied according to professional role, healthcare setting, and individual characteristics, including gender. Overall, EHR implementation provides important benefits for improving healthcare quality; however, it may also increase workload and reduce healthcare workers’ well-being when system usability is inadequate and digital tasks extend beyond regular working hours. Therefore, optimizing EHR design, simplifying documentation workflows, and limiting after-hours digital work are essential to support the long-term well-being of the healthcare workforce.

items.title: Death of Human Style of Writing in the World of AI
items.abstract: Abstract: The Artificial Intelligence (AI) writing tools like ChatGPT and Claude have changed the world of official and unofficial communication in last two to three years. The human style of writing is diminishing and there is a rise of only one universal writing style created by the AI tools which lack human expressions and creativity. The AI tools are rampantly used by students, researchers, writers and people in general for any kind of serious as well as casual writing today. The excessive use of AI tools in writing is also responsible for reducing human ability of logical and critical thinking. Therefore, there is an urgency of using AI writing tools wisely so that the human writing skills get enhanced and the tools prove to be a boon. This research paper examines the challenges posed by AI writing tools and discusses how the AI can be used effectively and responsibly to enhance human writing skills.

items.title: Death of Human Style of Writing in the World of AI
items.abstract: Abstract: The Artificial Intelligence (AI) writing tools like ChatGPT and Claude have changed the world of official and unofficial communication in last two to three years. The human style of writing is diminishing and there is a rise of only one universal writing style created by the AI tools which lack human expressions and creativity. The AI tools are rampantly used by students, researchers, writers and people in general for any kind of serious as well as casual writing today. The excessive use of AI tools in writing is also responsible for reducing human ability of logical and critical thinking. Therefore, there is an urgency of using AI writing tools wisely so that the human writing skills get enhanced and the tools prove to be a boon. This research paper examines the challenges posed by AI writing tools and discusses how the AI can be used effectively and responsibly to enhance human writing skills.

items.title: Debias It Yourself: Teaching LLMs Cognitive Bias Mitigation Interventions
items.abstract: Bias has long been studied in social psychology and cognitive science, where decades of research have produced a body of validated interventions that reduce stereotypical thinking and prejudiced responses in humans. We propose Debias It Yourself (DIY), a cognitively grounded framework that translates five such interventions into debiasing procedures for large language models and delivers them through three established paradigms: Show (in-context examples), Train (instruction tuning), and Revise (guided self-revision). Across three models, five bias benchmarks, eleven debiasing baselines, and three reasoning benchmarks, Train+Revise and Revise alone attain the top two average ranks, lead the bias-reasoning tradeoff (mean bias as low as 2% at 90% reasoning accuracy), and reduce bias on unseen dimensions by up to 14.8%. Our code and data are publicly available.

items.title: Delegating Knowledge: Belief in AI Sufficiency and its Consequences for How People Process Information
items.abstract: Generative AI produces information on demand, raising the question of why one would ever learn something that a chatbot can always retrieve. In this paper, we introduce Belief in AI Sufficiency (BAS): the belief that acquiring and retaining knowledge is less valuable because AI can provide it when needed. BAS represents a qualitatively distinct conceptual domain from the Google effect, cognitive offloading, and the “News Finds Me” perception. Using four preregistered studies in the United States (development, N = 307; validation, N = 903; experiment, N = 767; test-retest, N = 298), we present evidence for a 12-item BAS measure with a strong general factor structure. In the validation survey, higher BAS was associated with greater reliance on heuristic and less systematic processing, and with reduced factual knowledge. In the experiment, BAS strongly predicted the likelihood to delegate a learning task to AI. The relationship between BAS and the gap between self-reported and measured knowledge was smaller, reflecting reduced accuracy rather than an illusion of knowledge. Finally, BAS scores were approximately equal in mean level and showed moderate rank-order stability across a 3-month period. BAS is one way to measure how far AI is becoming central to the study of how people learn.

items.abstract: Research Question (RQ): How has research on AI and workload developed over time, and what themes, methods, and gaps shape current understanding of workload and well-being in AI-enabled work? Purpose: The purpose of this study is to map and describe the research landscape on AI and workload, identifying key topics, publication trends, and gaps relevant to work design, management, and well-being. Method: The study applies bibliometric analysis to peer-reviewed publications indexed in Scopus over the last five years. A transparent search strategy covers AI, workload, and related concepts. The analysis examines publication growth, citation patterns, source and author networks, and keyword co-occurrence, supported by science-mapping techniques. Interpretation is guided by work-design and job demands perspectives. Results: We found strong growth in publications across the AI and workload cross-section and high interdisciplinarity of the field. We reveal dominant research themes, the concentration of research across regions, and methodological patterns, as well as areas that remain understudied in relation to AI, workload, and well-being. Organization: By synthesizing a fragmented body of research, the study helps managers and HR professionals understand where evidence on the use of AI is well-developed and where caution or further evaluation is needed when implementing AI in work processes. Society: Clarifying how workload is addressed in AI-related research contributes to responsible AI use, worker health, and fair work practices in increasingly automated environments. Originality: The study offers a focused bibliometric overview of AI-related workload research, bringing together interdisciplinary perspectives on work design, stress, and well-being that are often studied separately. Limitations / further research: Bibliometric findings depend on coverage of a single database and on search choices and do not provide causal evidence. Future research should combine bibliometric mapping with empirical and intervention studies across sectors and regions.

items.title: Design for Cognitive Friction in Human-AI Interaction: A Student‑Centred AI Scaffold for Cognitive Resilience and Intellectual Agility
items.abstract: This exploratory, design-oriented pilot case study examines Erwin, a student-centred AI scaffold designed to augment students’ thinking in an interdisciplinary design innovation module. Unlike answer-giving chatbots, Erwin adopts a supportive-critic stance: it provides stage-aware, dialogic scaffolding that widens idea spaces and supports criteria-based consolidation through nudges and commitments. The analysis drew on 1,999 student and Erwin turns organised into 171 sessions nested within 78 student logs, alongside post-module qualitative feedback. The study combined reflexive thematic analysis with a full-corpus, non-inferential descriptive analysis of selected interaction-process indicators, including initiative balance, futures probes, completed repair sequences, and system boundary or refusal episodes. A purposive sample of six final artefacts provided illustrative triangulation of interaction patterns and student project trajectories. The analysis identified four practices: disciplined divergence, in which Deliberate Cognitive Friction (DCF) prompts appeared alongside expanded frames without displacing agency; criteria-aware convergence, in which students translated broadened views into clearer problem statements, constraints, and next steps; cognitive resilience visible through repair and persistence sequences; and a supportive-critic experience shaped by answer resistance and meta-reflection. As this was a single-course pilot with no control condition, the descriptive indicators characterise observed interaction processes and contextualise the qualitative interpretation; they are not estimates of causal effects or direct measures of learning outcomes. Across cases, these practices appeared alongside traces of broadened ideation, criteria-guided consolidation, and futures-oriented reasoning in the illustrative artefact sample. The paper contributes situated empirical evidence for studying AI as human augmentation rather than substitution; a transferable design blueprint that operationalises DCF at the prompt policy layer through explainable prompts, resilience guardrails, and instrumentation for scaffolding-oriented LLM systems; and a process-oriented operationalisation of cognitive resilience for Human Computer Interaction in education, understood as interactional evidence of repair, persistence, and flexible reframing rather than as a demonstrated learning effect. The discussion offers implications for designing resilient, trust-preserving human-AI ecosystems that balance augmentation against risks of overreliance and cognitive offloading.

items.title: Determining key approaches to enhancing the survivability of armored vehicle crews, considering the use of situational awareness systems in modern warfare
items.abstract: The study aims to provide a theoretical rationale for key approaches to enhancing the survivability of armored vehicle crews–incorporating situational awareness systems–and to develop a novel method for assessing the extent to which these systems contribute to the crew's defensive response. The methodological framework combines systems, structural-functional, comparative, and criteria-based approaches, alongside a content analysis of scholarly works, the decomposition of the situational awareness cycle, and a custom point-based assessment method. Crew survivability is viewed as the outcome of the coordinated operation of systems for observation, threat detection, identification and prioritization, information exchange, decision support, protection, and the restoration of control following adverse impacts. It is established that situational awareness serves a preventive function within the survivability system of armored vehicles, as it shifts the initiation of the defensive response to a stage preceding the actual impact. A six-criterion assessment system is proposed, covering the continuity and completeness of observation, timeliness of detection, resilience of information support, quality of prioritization, integration of information exchange, and the capacity to sustain the crew's defensive response. A 0–4 point scale and an integral index are used to compare the conceptual approaches. The scientific novelty lies in interpreting situational awareness as a functional component of ensuring crew survival through preventive measures and in formulating the "perception–recognition–assessment–decision–protective reaction" sequence as an object of theoretical evaluation. The practical significance of the results stems from their potential application in substantiating modernization directions for armored weaponry and equipment, preliminarily comparing information support options, and establishing development priorities for situational awareness systems.

items.title: Developing an AI Governance Readiness Index (AIGRI) for Indian Higher Education Institutions
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education with intelligent learning systems, automated administration, research support, academic assessment, and institutional decision-making. As Indian Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) increasingly incorporate AI-enabled technologies, the lack of a standardized framework for evaluating institutional readiness for responsible AI governance has become a significant policy and administrative challenge. Current evaluation mechanisms primarily emphasize digital infrastructure and technology adoption, neglecting critical aspects such as ethical governance, institutional policy, regulatory compliance, data governance, academic integrity, human capacity development, and transparency, accountability, and risk management. In this paper, we propose developing an AI Governance Readiness Index (AIGRI) as a multidimensional framework to evaluate the preparedness of Indian Higher Education Institutions for the responsible and sustainable adoption of AI. The proposed index is structured around eight interconnected dimensions: Institutional Leadership and Governance, AI Policy and Regulatory Compliance, Digital Infrastructure, Data Governance and Cybersecurity, Human Capacity and AI Literacy, Ethical and Responsible AI Practices, Academic and Research Integrity, and Continuous Evaluation and Innovation. Each dimension is associated with measurable indicators that enable institutions to assess their current status, identify governance gaps, and formulate evidence-based strategies for improvement. The study employs a qualitative doctrinal and policy research approach, underpinned by an extensive review of national education policies, AI governance frameworks, international ethical AI guidelines, and literature on higher education quality assurance. The paper proposes a preliminary scoring model based on principles of responsible AI, good governance, and institutional accountability, which can then be validated through empirical research with universities across India. The proposed AIGRI is a practical governance tool for university administrators, policymakers, accreditation agencies, and regulatory bodies to assess AI readiness systematically. It also contributes to the emerging discourse of AI governance by shifting the focus from technology adoption to institutional preparedness, ethical implementation, and governance maturity. The framework could be a valuable addition to national quality assurance efforts, such as NAAC. It could be aligned with India’s vision of digitally empowered, globally competitive, and socially responsible higher education institutions. The study concludes that the development of a standardized AI Governance Readiness Index can guide policy decisions, enhance institutional resilience, encourage responsible AI adoption, and aid sustainable transformation of higher education in the era of intelligent technologies.

items.title: Development and Validation of the Occupational Safety Awareness Scale for Motorcycle Couriers
items.abstract: Motorcycle couriers in the platform-based gig economy are exposed to substantial occupational risks, yet no validated instrument exists to measure their occupational health and safety (OHS) awareness. This study develops and validates the Occupational Safety Awareness Scale for Motorcycle Couriers (OSAS-MC) to address this gap. Drawing on Türkiye’s OHS Law No. 6331, international OHS standards, and feedback from five domain experts, an initial item pool was generated and refined into a 30-item, six-dimensional instrument covering OHS Legislation Knowledge, OHS Practices, Personal Protective Equipment Use, Motorbike Use, OHS Exposure, and OHS Risk Factors. The scale was administered to 265 actively employed motorcycle couriers in Türkiye. Exploratory factor analysis supported a six-factor solution explaining 67.79% of the variance, and confirmatory factor analysis indicated an acceptable model fit (CFI = 0.875; RMSEA = 0.076; χ²/df = 2.543). Internal consistency was high overall (Cronbach’s α = 0.878) and across sub-dimensions (α = 0.805–0.895), and item discrimination was confirmed via upper-lower 27% group comparisons. The OSAS-MC offers a reliable, context-sensitive instrument for assessing safety awareness in high-risk, platform-mediated delivery work, and provides policymakers, platform operators, and labour organisations with a diagnostic tool to identify awareness gaps and guide targeted interventions.

items.title: Development of An English Language Learning Model Through Gamification Technology for Higher Education
items.abstract: This study investigated higher education instructors' needs regarding gamified English language learning and developed an Applied Linguistics-informed instructional model for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction. Grounded in Second Language Acquisition (SLA) theory—including Gardner's (1985) motivation framework, Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) principles, and Self-Determination Theory (SDT)—the study employed an Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation (ADDIE)-guided Design and Development Research (DDR) approach. A purposive sample of 158 EFL instructors completed a validated 15-item questionnaire (IOC = 0.80–1.00; α = 0.81). Findings indicated strong support for gamification in promoting communicative engagement, learner autonomy, and intrinsic motivation. Based on these findings, a five-component gamification-integrated model was developed and evaluated by five experts using an 11-item instrument (α = 0.85), achieving an overall mean rating of 4.60 (very high). The study contributes to Applied Linguistics and English language education by presenting an SLA-informed model that operationalizes gamification as a structured communicative pedagogy rather than isolated game mechanics, offering an empirically informed and theoretically grounded framework for EFL instruction in Thai higher education.

items.title: Digital technologies and mental health in young people in higher education
items.abstract: Abstract: Scientific literature has shown an association between the use of digital technologies and the mental health of higher education students. However, gaps remain regarding the digital practices used to promote mental health literacy. In this context, a qualitative study was conducted using six focus groups, involving 43 students from 32 courses at 18 Portuguese higher education institutions. Thematic analysis of the data identified five themes: Digital habits; Digital technologies in mentalhealth literacy; Impact of digital technologies on well-being and mental health; Evaluation of digital technologies in mental health; Good practices in promoting well-being and mental health. The results show that the focus groups provided spaces for critical reflection and collective construction of knowledge concerning the benefits, risks and limitations of digital technologies in mental health. However, a discrepancy was identified between the participants’ critical discourse and their actualpractices. Despite reservations about the use of non-specialist digital tools, there is widespread reliance on social media content and artificial intelligence. This finding highlights a focus on immediacy, anonymity and accessibility, underscoring the need to gain a better understanding of these mechanisms and to improve access to specialist services.

items.title: DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES AND STUDENT-CENTERED LEARNING IN MODERN HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: The digital transformation of education has significantly changed approaches to teaching and learning in higher education. Traditional teacher-centered instruction is increasingly being supplemented by interactive, personalized, and student-centered learning models supported by digital technologies. This article examines the pedagogical potential of learning management systems, digital communication platforms, artificial intelligence tools, multimedia resources, virtual learning environments, and online assessment technologies. The study employs theoretical analysis and synthesis of contemporary educational research. The results suggest that digital technologies can strengthen students’ autonomy, collaboration, critical thinking, motivation, and access to educational resources when they are integrated according to clearly defined pedagogical objectives. At the same time, excessive dependence on technology, digital inequality, academic integrity problems, information overload, and insufficient digital competence among educators remain important challenges. The paper argues that the effectiveness of educational digitalization depends not on the quantity of technological tools but on their pedagogically appropriate application. Keywords: digital education, student-centered learning, higher education, educational technology, digital competence, active learning, pedagogy

items.title: Digital Transformation of Disaster Response in Wajima City Following the 2024 Noto Peninsula Earthquake: Implementation Process and Operational Conditions —A Comparative Case Analysis of Five Operations—
items.abstract: This study examines the implementation process and operational conditions determining the success or failure of the digital transformation of disaster response in Wajima City, Ishikawa Prefecture, following the 2024 Noto Peninsula Earthquake. The study is based on a single-case comparative analysis of five operations—post-earthquake building safety assessment, shelter management, temporary housing, facility management, and publicly funded demolition—using operational records, products, meeting materials, and development logs. These operations were compared using five dimensions: digitalization of information collection, accumulation of shareable data, situational awareness through visualization, connection to decision support, and cross-departmental coordination. Among the five operations, post-earthquake building safety assessment and temporary housing advanced most continuously, while shelter management and facility management tended to remain at the stage of visualization, and publicly funded demolition remained fragmented. The results reveal that the digital transformation of disaster response progressed step by step from data input to accumulation, visualization, and decision support, rather than emerging all at once. Self-contained operations tended to advance more smoothly, whereas cross-departmental operations required clearer coordination and decision-making mechanisms. Thus, success depended less on technology itself than on operational conditions, implying that effective implementation depends on the peacetime preparation of data items, identifiers, update responsibilities, and decision-making arrangements.

items.title: DPMF: A Dynamic Risk-Aware Permission Framework for Securing AI Agents Using Third-Party APIs
items.abstract: AI agents are moving from systems that only generate information to systems that can plan tasks, use tools, and perform operations through external APIs. This shift creates a security problem that traditional permission models do not fully address: an agent may hold broad privileges even when a particular task needs only a small part of that access. A valid token therefore does not automatically mean that every action produced by the agent is appropriate. This paper proposes DPMF (Dynamic Risk-Aware Permission Framework), an external authorization layer for AI agents that interact with third-party services. DPMF evaluates each proposed API action using contextual signals such as user-intent alignment, data sensitivity, permission severity, source trust, action reversibility, and behavioral deviation. The resulting risk level drives one of four decisions: Allow, Restrict, Human Approval, or Deny. The framework also separates the agent's ability to propose an action from the security layer's authority to approve it. The paper presents the framework architecture, threat model, risk-scoring approach, dynamic permission algorithm, case study, and an experimental methodology for comparing DPMF with static authorization. Because the framework has not yet been experimentally implemented, no numerical performance claims are presented as established results. Instead, measurable evaluation criteria and expected outcomes are defined.

items.title: Driving the future: Evaluating a training concept for advanced driver assistance systems
items.abstract: With the widespread adoption of Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems (ADAS), the need for effective ADAS driver training increases. However, empirical evidence regarding the effectiveness of ADAS education remains limited. This study evaluated the effectiveness of an ADAS driver training program across four European countries. The training included classroom-based theoretical instruction and practical hands-on experience on test-tracks and open-roads. 166 participants completed a questionnaire measuring their knowledge, attitudes, and behavioral intentions towards ADAS pre- and post-training. Overall knowledge of system purpose, handling and limitations improved significantly with the training. However, some misunderstandings remained, and in some cases, misconceptions from before the training were not corrected. Perceived safety and trust remained unchanged while willingness to use ADAS systems, and the perceived ease of use and usefulness of ADAS increased. Future training should not only provide information for trainees but also identify misconceptions they may hold. Follow-up or feedback sessions are recommended to address potential misunderstandings.

items.title: Educommunication and artificial intelligence for learning, creating, and communicating: professional competency development in university prosumers
items.abstract: Introduction This study examines the pedagogical integration of educommunication and artificial intelligence (AI) and its association with self-reported professional competencies among university prosumers-students who simultaneously consume, produce, and share academic content through digital platforms. Methods A non-experimental, cross-sectional quantitative design with descriptive-correlational and structural purposes was employed. Data were collected using a psychometrically validated 26-item Likert-scale questionnaire (plus six open-response items) administered to a convenience sample of 547 university students enrolled at Universidad Politécnica Salesiana, Ecuador. The instrument assessed five dimensions: (1) AI-mediated learning processes, (2) educommunication and expression, (3) knowledge prosumption, (4) perceived professional competencies, and (5) ethics and critical AI use. Psychometric validation confirmed excellent reliability (Cronbach's α = 0.91; McDonald's ω = 0.93). Exploratory factor analysis supported the five-factor structure (Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin [KMO] = 0.91; Bartlett's test p < 0.001; variance explained = 61.4%). Confirmatory factor analysis indicated a satisfactory model fit (comparative fit index [CFI] = 0.96; Tucker-Lewis index [TLI] = 0.95; root mean square error of approximation [RMSEA] = 0.052; standardized root mean square residual [SRMR] = 0.061). A single-factor test yielded a first unrotated factor accounting for 28.3% of the variance, below the 50% threshold, offering a preliminary indication against a single dominant method factor, although this test alone does not rule out common method bias (see Section 3.3). Results Structural equation modeling revealed significant direct paths from AI-mediated learning to perceived professional competencies ( β = 0.58, p < 0.001) and from educommunication to knowledge prosumption ( β = 0.51, p < 0.001), with knowledge prosumption partially mediating the educommunication-competency association ( β _indirect = 0.21; R² = 0.74 for D3; R² = 0.78 for D4), and ethics and critical AI use functioning as a significant moderator of the AI learning-competency path (interaction β = 0.34, p < 0.001). Given the cross-sectional, self-report design, these results are interpreted as structural associations rather than causal effects. Discussion Findings indicate that AI integration within educommunicative frameworks is positively associated with autonomous learning, creativity, and digital communication skills. However, risks associated with technological over-reliance and epistemic dependency were also identified in the qualitative data. These findings constitute structurally validated evidence that pedagogical AI integration, framed within educommunicative approaches, is associated with the perceived development of critical, collaborative, and innovative professional competencies in higher education.
