items.title: Effectiveness of AI-Supported Learning in English Vocabulary Acquisition among Undergraduate Learners: A Quasi-Experimental Study
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines the effectiveness of structured AI-supported learning in English vocabulary acquisition among undergraduate learners. A quasi-experimental design involved two intact B.A. Part-I student divisions at Shri Vijaysinha Yadav College, Peth Vadgaon. Both groups received instruction covering 100 target vocabulary items in four areas. The Experimental Group received teacher-guided support through an AI-Supported Vocabulary Learning Cycle using NotebookLM and ChatGPT for learning, practice, feedback, and revision. Both groups subsequently completed the same 100 item vocabulary post-test. Independent samples t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and Cohen’s d were used. The Experimental Group achieved a significantly higher overall mean score (75.53) than the Control Group (66.95), t(70) = 6.39, p < .001, d = 1.51. All four categories showed significant differences, strongest for phrasal verbs. Gender showed no significant difference, whereas previous AI exposure and regular smartphone use were associated with higher achievement among Experimental Group learners. The findings suggest that AI can contribute to vocabulary learning when carefully and purposefully integrated with teacher-led classroom instruction and curriculum objectives. AI extends practice, feedback, revision, and application. Overall findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the intact-group design and absence of delayed assessment.

items.title: Effectiveness of occupational safety and health training in virtual reality: a comparative study with traditional methods
items.abstract: This article analyses the effectiveness and perception of occupational safety and health (OSH) training using virtual reality (VR) compared to traditional methods. The aim of the study was to verify the effectiveness of VR training compared to traditional methods (Research No. 1) and to analyse the impressions of participants with different experiences with VR in the training system (Research No. 2). Research No. 1, conducted on students in the fields of construction and occupational health and safety, compared test results after traditional training (in person / online training) and VR (the “VR training at work at height” application). Research No. 2 included active construction workers, analysing their opinions on the usefulness, engagement, and impact of VR training on hazard knowledge, using questionnaires and participant observation. Research No. 1’s results showed a significant improvement in test scores after VRtraining (an average increase of 22%), suggesting a higher effectiveness of this method. In Research No. 2, participants rated highly the usefulness of VR in health and safety training, comfort with VR devices, and their own participation. The results of the study confirm the effectiveness of VR training in occupational safety and health, increasing the effectiveness and participation of participants. Immersion, visualisation, and simulation of harsh working conditions are key advantages of this technology. The VR training system combines the experience of virtual reality with learning theory, simulating emergency response procedures and procedures for the use of personal protective equipment.

items.title: Effects of Job Satisfaction on the Performance of Employees in Various Industries
items.abstract: Job satisfaction is widely recognised as a critical determinant of employee performance, organisational productivity, and long-term institutional effectiveness across diverse economic sectors. This paper examines the relationship between job satisfaction and employee performance through a comparative lens that considers both developed and developing country contexts. Drawing on a systematic literature review of empirical studies published between 2015 and 2025, the study synthesises evidence from a broad range of industries, including education, telecommunications, banking and financial services, information technology, automotive, healthcare, retail, construction, agriculture, logistics, energy, public administration, and manufacturing.The findings reveal a consistently positive and statistically significant association between job satisfaction and employee performance, either directly or through mediating mechanisms such as work engagement, organisational commitment, and motivation. Across sectors, job satisfaction is shaped by a combination of structural and motivational factors, including working conditions, training and development, leadership quality, compensation, career advancement opportunities, organisational support, and job design. Employees who report higher satisfaction levels tend to demonstrate stronger commitment, greater discretionary effort, higher productivity, and improved service quality.

items.title: ENGLISH-MAJOR STUDENTS’ PERCEPTIONS OF AI-ASSISTED IELTS WRITING TASK 2 PRACTICE IN HIGHER EDUCATION: A QUALITATIVE STUDY AT THANH DO UNIVERSITY, VIETNAM
items.abstract: This study investigated English-major students’ perceptions of AI-assisted tools in IELTS Writing Task 2 practice at Thanh Do University, Vietnam. The study aimed to explore how students perceived the usefulness and challenges of using AI-assisted writing technologies during IELTS-oriented writing activities. A qualitative research design was employed, involving semi-structured interviews with 15 third-year English-major students enrolled in the Integrated English 2 course during the second semester of the 2025 academic year. The participants had experience using AI-assisted tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, and Gemini to support IELTS Writing Task 2 practice. Interview data were analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings revealed that students generally perceived AI-assisted writing tools positively due to their usefulness in idea generation, essay organization, grammar correction, vocabulary enhancement, and self-study support. Participants also believed that AI technologies improved writing confidence and encouraged learner autonomy. However, concerns regarding overreliance on AI-generated content, reduced independent thinking, and the reliability of AI-generated feedback were also identified. The study highlights the potential of AI-assisted writing technologies as supplementary learning resources in IELTS-oriented writing instruction while emphasizing the importance of responsible and balanced AI integration in higher education contexts.

items.title: ENHANCING STUDENT ENGAGEMENT THROUGH AI-BASED LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS
items.abstract: This conference paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI)-based learning environments can enhance student engagement in higher education. The study focuses on the integration of learning analytics, recommendation systems, intelligent tutoring, adaptive feedback, and interactive programming tasks to support behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and social engagement. The proposed model links learner profiling, real-time analytics, personalization, feedback, and pedagogical design into a unified engagement-oriented learning environment. A model-based experimental framework is presented with sample indicators and illustrative results. The findings suggest that AI-supported adaptive learning environments may increase student participation, improve persistence in programming tasks, strengthen self-regulated learning, and support the development of programming competence. The paper also discusses implementation challenges, including data privacy, teacher readiness, infrastructure, and the need for human-centered AI design. Keywords: artificial intelligence, student engagement, AI-based learning environment, learning analytics, adaptive feedback, personalized learning

items.title: Enter the Agentomaly: How Billions of Personal AI Agents Will Become the New Economy
items.abstract: Persistent personal AI agents may change the relationship between an individual's attention and productive capacity. This paper defines Agentomaly as a proposed transition in which individuals can affordably sustain adaptive, concurrent delegated work that previously required more direct attention or organizational support. Delegation and automation are not new. The hypothesis concerns a change in their accessibility, flexibility, persistence, and coordination cost at the level of the individual principal. The paper distinguishes three questions: whether agents expand individual productive capacity; whether their interactions become a substantial operational layer of the economy; and whether the resulting systems preserve meaningful human authority. These outcomes need not coincide. A closed platform could deliver large productivity gains while concentrating control and making exit difficult. The proposed analytical unit is the principal-agent relationship. Its performance should be evaluated through quality-adjusted completed outcomes, principal attention, total human labor, elapsed time, resource cost, and externalities. More agent activity is not evidence of more economic value. The paper also develops the Principal Concentration Problem: many agent identities may represent one controlling organization rather than independent market participants. A governance framework addresses bounded mandates, audit, continuity, portability, and human re-entry. These are design commitments to assess separately from productivity, not assumed consequences of technical capability. A research agenda proposes comparisons with manual work, AI-assisted work, conventional automation, and human delegation. The 2030 horizon is a scenario boundary, not a forecast. The contribution is an integrated framework for testing when persistent delegation expands individual agency, how its benefits and costs are distributed, and whether its expansion remains subject to effective human control.

items.title: Enter the Agentomaly: How Billions of Personal AI Agents Will Become the New Economy
items.abstract: Persistent personal AI agents may change the relationship between an individual's attention and productive capacity. This paper defines Agentomaly as a proposed transition in which individuals can affordably sustain adaptive, concurrent delegated work that previously required more direct attention or organizational support. Delegation and automation are not new. The hypothesis concerns a change in their accessibility, flexibility, persistence, and coordination cost at the level of the individual principal. The paper distinguishes three questions: whether agents expand individual productive capacity; whether their interactions become a substantial operational layer of the economy; and whether the resulting systems preserve meaningful human authority. These outcomes need not coincide. A closed platform could deliver large productivity gains while concentrating control and making exit difficult. The proposed analytical unit is the principal-agent relationship. Its performance should be evaluated through quality-adjusted completed outcomes, principal attention, total human labor, elapsed time, resource cost, and externalities. More agent activity is not evidence of more economic value. The paper also develops the Principal Concentration Problem: many agent identities may represent one controlling organization rather than independent market participants. A governance framework addresses bounded mandates, audit, continuity, portability, and human re-entry. These are design commitments to assess separately from productivity, not assumed consequences of technical capability. A research agenda proposes comparisons with manual work, AI-assisted work, conventional automation, and human delegation. The 2030 horizon is a scenario boundary, not a forecast. The contribution is an integrated framework for testing when persistent delegation expands individual agency, how its benefits and costs are distributed, and whether its expansion remains subject to effective human control.

items.title: Ethical Frameworks and Guideline for the Conceptualisation and Use of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Health Innovations in Nursing Education and Practice: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Background and rationale Digital health technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly transforming healthcare delivery, health professional education, clinical decision-making, workforce development, and health-system organisation. The World Health Organization (WHO) recognises digital health as an important mechanism for strengthening health systems and improving access to equitable, efficient and high-quality healthcare (World Health Organization [WHO], 2025a), reflecting the continuing importance of digital health transformation globally (WHO, 2025b). AI has particular potential to influence clinical decision-making, service delivery, education and research. In nursing and midwifery, AI technologies have been applied across direct patient care, administration and management, and, to a lesser extent, education. A systematic review by O’Connor et al. (2023) identified 140 studies involving applications of AI to nursing and midwifery, with most applications directed towards clinical practice and patient care. However, the review also identified important limitations and risks, including poor-quality datasets and potential bias, privacy and trust concerns, the need for clinical interpretation of AI-generated results, and limited AI expertise among nurses and midwives. These findings demonstrate that implementation of AI is not solely a technological issue but also has professional, educational, ethical and governance implications. The rapid adoption of AI and other digital technologies creates opportunities to improve healthcare access, efficiency, clinical decision-making and patient outcomes, while simultaneously raising significant ethical, legal and social concerns. The WHO has emphasised that ethics and human rights should be central to the design, development, deployment and use of AI for health (WHO, 2021). Its guidance identifies principles including protecting human autonomy; promoting the public interest; ensuring transparency, explainability and intelligibility; fostering responsibility and accountability; and promoting AI that is responsive and sustainable. These principles highlight the importance of considering ethics throughout the lifecycle of health technologies rather than only after technologies have been implemented. Ethical considerations are especially important in nursing because nurses have sustained interactions with patients and families and frequently engage with health information systems, digital technologies and clinical decision-support tools at the point of care. The increasing incorporation of AI into nursing therefore raises questions concerning professional accountability, autonomy, informed consent, privacy and confidentiality, data security, algorithmic bias, transparency, equity, patient safety, trust and preservation of human-centred care (Badawy et al., 2025; Mohammed et al., 2025). Ethical issues are also emerging in nursing education as generative AI becomes increasingly accessible to students and educators. De Gagne et al. (2024) argue that the integration of AI into nursing education requires consideration of established ethical principles, including autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, justice and explicability. They emphasise the need for ethical principles to be incorporated into curricula and for appropriate guidance to support responsible AI use. Other nursing education literature has similarly identified potential benefits of AI and AI-enabled chatbots for personalised learning, simulation, accessibility and educator support, alongside concerns relating to privacy, confidentiality, bias and appropriate use (Srinivasan et al., 2024). Despite increasing recognition of these issues, the evidence relevant to nursing remains dispersed across different technologies, settings, populations and types of ethical consideration. Existing reviews demonstrate that ethical challenges associated with AI in nursing are substantial (Badawy et al., 2025; Mohammed et al., 2025), while broader reviews demonstrate considerable variation in how AI is being introduced and evaluated across nursing and midwifery practice (O’Connor et al., 2023). However, identifying ethical concerns alone does not establish what ethical frameworks, guidelines, principles or governance approaches are being used to guide the conceptualisation and application of these technologies, nor how such guidance is operationalised in nursing education and practice. There is therefore a need to systematically map primary research addressing the ethical conceptualisation and application of AI and digital health innovations within nursing. In particular, it is important to identify the ethical guidelines, frameworks, principles and empirically derived recommendations reported in the literature; describe their underlying characteristics and intended applications; and examine the factors associated with their implementation or application in nursing education and practice. Such mapping can clarify the current evidence base, identify areas of convergence and inconsistency, reveal gaps between ethical principles and their practical implementation, and identify priorities for future nursing research, education, professional guidance and governance. Accordingly, this scoping review aims to map how AI and digital health innovations are conceptualised and applied ethically in nursing practice and education. A scoping review is appropriate because the purpose is to examine the breadth and characteristics of the available evidence, identify the ethical frameworks and principles represented across heterogeneous primary studies, and explore factors associated with their application rather than determine the effectiveness of a single intervention. Aim: The overall aim of this scoping review is to map how artificial intelligence and digital health innovations are conceptualised and applied ethically in nursing practice and education. The review will additionally map, where reported: • the characteristics and underlying ethical principles of identified guidelines, frameworks or recommendations; • the types of AI and digital health technologies to which ethical considerations are applied; • the nursing settings and populations in which these considerations arise; • the intended or actual applications of identified ethical guidance in nursing education and clinical practice; and • barriers, facilitators and other contextual considerations associated with ethical implementation and use. items.abstract: Fairness is one of the fundamental ethical principles governing the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education. AI systems increasingly influence learning recommendations, assessment, student support, admissions, academic advising, and institutional decision-making. Because these systems can affect educational opportunities, fairness must be considered throughout their design, development, deployment, and evaluation. An AI system is not automatically fair simply because it uses mathematical or computational methods. If the data, assumptions, objectives, or decision processes contain bias, the resulting system may reproduce or amplify existing inequalities. A simplified framework is: Educational Data → AI Model → Prediction/Recommendation → Educational Decision → Student Outcome Fairness requires examining every stage of this process. Fairness in AI-based education refers to the principle that learners should be treated equitably and should not experience unjustified disadvantage because of characteristics unrelated to legitimate educational objectives.Fairness involves: Equal opportunity Non-discrimination Appropriate treatment Inclusive access Consistent evaluation Protection from unjustified bias Fairness does not always mean treating every learner identically. Different learners may require different forms of support to achieve equitable educational opportunities. The major objectives include: Reducing discriminatory outcomes Providing equitable educational opportunities Identifying and reducing algorithmic bias Supporting inclusive learning Ensuring equitable access to AI systems Protecting vulnerable learners Promoting trustworthy educational technologies Fairness should be considered throughout: Data Collection → Model Development → Testing → Deployment → Monitoring A system that is fair during development may produce unfair outcomes after deployment if the educational environment changes. AI systems learn from data. If historical educational data contain unequal patterns, an AI system may reproduce them. For example: Historical Bias → Training Data → AI Model → Potentially Biased Prediction

items.title: EurekaBench: Measuring Agentic Ability to Discover New Scientific Insights
items.abstract: When Isaac Newton discovered the law of gravitation, he did so through an iterative process of analyzing observed data such as planetary patterns, finding the underlying mechanisms by describing patterns in mathematical equations, and refining his theory against the Moon's orbit, revealing the startling insight that the same force governs both falling apples and orbiting planets. Would it be possible for AI agents to make similar discoveries? To measure this ability, we introduce EurekaBench, a cross-domain benchmark that tests AI agents' ability to conduct long-horizon experiments and discover mechanisms that explain observations. We evaluate these mechanisms by the scientific insights that can be derived from them. EurekaBench contains an expert-verified set of 26 long-horizon tasks across neuroscience, computer science, chemistry, astrophysics, geophysics, and plasma physics, with a total of 306 scientific insights that the discovered mechanisms are expected to support. Our evaluation framework tests three axes of scientific discovery: agents' ability to follow known scientific constraints, the predictive accuracy of the discovered mechanisms, and whether these mechanisms yield scientific insights or inform future research. Our results show that current AI agents often overly fixate on predictive accuracy optimization, surpassing human scientists, while falling substantially short in deriving scientific insights.

items.title: Evaluating Agentic AI: The Multi-Layer Evaluation Model (MLE-A)
items.abstract: The emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) marks a shift from reactive educational technologies towards systems capable of autonomous multi-step planning, tool orchestration, and adaptive decision-making. As these systems contribute to structuring study pathways, generating feedback, and monitoring learner progression, elements of cognitive and metacognitive regulation become distributed between learners and AI agents. However, existing evaluation approaches in educational technology remain largely focused on usability, performance, and satisfaction, and are therefore insufficient to capture these dynamic and distributed forms of agency. This paper proposes the Multi-Layer Evaluation Model for Agentic AI (MLE-A), a conceptual framework for assessing the educational impact of agentic systems across five interacting dimensions: cognitive, metacognitive, affective, behavioural, and system-level governance. The model provides a structured basis for analysing human–AI collaboration and supporting future empirical evaluation.

items.title: Evaluating AI chatbots for providing health advice on occupational sedentary behavior in the workplace
items.abstract: Background Office workers accumulate most of their waking h in sedentary behavior, yet scalable personalized occupational-health advice remains limited, and the quality of large language model (LLM)-based tools in this domain has not been rigorously examined. Objective This study evaluated whether a domain-specialized chatbot system for providing health advice on sedentary behavior, integrating retrieval augmentation, a curated corpus, and safety guardrails, performs better than a general-purpose LLM and static educational materials. Methods A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was used. In the blinded expert evaluation, nine raters independently rated 60 responses across five quality dimensions. In the user survey, 654 eligible Chinese office workers interacted with the specialized chatbot and completed six perception scales (two adapted from established technology-acceptance frameworks and four developed for this study) plus open-ended feedback. Results Inter-rater reliability was good for the composite score; in a case-level safety screen, no response from the specialized chatbot or the standard materials was flagged as potentially unsafe, whereas two Doubao responses were flagged by two or more raters. The specialized chatbot achieved the highest composite rating, followed by Doubao and standard materials. In a linear mixed-effects model and crossed random intercepts for rater and question, all Holm-adjusted pairwise contrasts were significant. Advantages of the specialized chatbot over Doubao were most pronounced on safety in symptom-management and special-population items. Among users, perceived ease of use was highest, whereas perceived safety and intention to use were rated comparatively lower. Nonetheless, users remained cautious about safety and intention to use after this brief exposure.

items.title: Evaluating The Impact of An Ai-Driven Clinical Decision Support System on Nursing Students' Accuracy in Care-Plan Formulation During Telemedicine Practicum
items.abstract: Care-plan formulation is among the most cognitively demanding competencies that pre-registration nursing students must master, and errors made at this formative stage may persist into qualified practice. Two contemporary developments converge on this competency: the emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) capable of suggesting nursing diagnoses and interventions, and the normalization of the telemedicine practicum as a clinical learning environment. No prior synthesis has examined their intersection. The aim of this study is to identify, appraise, and synthesize the evidence on the effect of AI-driven CDSS on the accuracy of nursing students’ care-plan formulation within telemedicine practicum settings. The review is designed and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement and conducted with reference to the Cochrane Handbook and the JBI Manual for Evidence Synthesis. Eight databases and grey-literature sources searched for peer-reviewed English-language studies published between 2015 and 2026. Screening, extraction, and appraisal were performed in duplicate; risk of bias was assessed with design-appropriate instruments (RoB 2, ROBINS-I, JBI checklists, MMAT), and certainty was rated using GRADE. Heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis, and a structured narrative synthesis following SWiM guidance was undertaken. The evidence converges on a conditional benefit. Structured, taxonomy-aligned decision support raised students’ diagnostic and care-plan accuracy relative to unsupported practice, with the inference model, the supervision arrangement, and learner characteristics acting as decisive moderators. Generative large language models produced substantial gains in rated plan quality but exhibited a characteristic failure mode of fluent yet taxonomy-discordant output, creating conditions in which automation bias is most hazardous. The telemedicine setting amplified both the potential benefit and the risk of uncritical reliance. The study concludes that an AI-driven CDSS functions as a conditional cognitive scaffold rather than an unconditional accelerator of accuracy. Its educational value in the telemedicine practicum is realized only where outputs are aligned with recognized nursing taxonomies, system reasoning is transparent, and use is embedded within supervised, deliberate practice that preserves the student as the accountable clinical reasoner. Recommendations are made for nursing education, policy, and future primary research.

items.title: Exception Exposure Deprivation and Emergency Readiness Vulnerability among Seafarers in Highly Standardized Ship Operations
items.abstract: Modern ship operations use strict procedures and advanced automation, which may reduce seafarers’ experience in handling unexpected situations. This study aims to analyze the relationship between exception exposure deprivation and emergency readiness vulnerability among seafarers. A quantitative correlational method was conducted through a questionnaire survey involving 100 seafarers and maritime trainees in Banten, Indonesia. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, validity and reliability tests, Pearson correlation, and simple linear regression. The results indicate that limited exposure to abnormal situations is associated with lower emergency readiness among seafarers. This study highlights the importance of realistic emergency training and varied scenarios to improve maritime safety and human performance.

items.title: Executive Judgement in AI-Mediated Decision-Making Environments: A Process Theory of Formation, Qualification Attrition and Authorisation
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can contribute to the representations, alternatives and evaluations through which executive judgements are formed. Existing research already explains important aspects of hybrid cognition, reliance, managerial agency and accountability. This article develops a narrower process challenge: locally competent human and AI contributions can still culminate in an inadequately warranted organisational commitment when established operational assumptions, uncertainties or dependencies are lost or transformed before authorisation. It proposes qualification attrition as the process through which such epistemically consequential content is weakened across successive transformations, and a formation--authorisation gap as the resulting discrepancy between the grounds required for warranted commitment and those that remain accessible, intelligible and challengeable to the authorising role. Executive judgement governance is defined through four dimensions: boundary setting, interpretive challenge, reliance calibration, and authorisation with answerability. Four propositions connect transformation, qualification attrition and governance arrangements to epistemic risk, accountability risk and judgement quality. The contribution is an integrative process theory of how distributed judgement formation can fail as a composition even where individual contributions, local reliance decisions and formal accountability arrangements appear competent.

items.title: Exploring the Impact of Technological Readiness, Teaching Supports, and Peer Interaction on Cognitive Presence and Learning Outcomes in TVET-Based Smart Grid Engineering Education
items.abstract: Electronics Engineering is rapidly transforming into a sustainable digital-based system. This requires engineers to continuously strive to develop cognitive, self-regulation, and technological competencies. This study examines the influence of Technology Readiness (TR), Instructional Support (TS), and Peer Interaction (PI) on Cognitive Presence (CP) and Learning Outcomes (LO). Learning Outcomes are achieved after first going through the mediation role of Self Regulatory Learning (SRL) and Cognitive Engagement (CE) in Smart Grid Engineering Education. This study involved 120 undergraduate students. We applied Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4 in the data analysis. The results showed that Teaching Support significantly predicted Peer Interaction, Self-Regulatory Learning, and Technology Readiness, indicating its important role in teaching. Self-Regulatory Learning positively influenced Cognitive Engagement, which in turn strengthened Cognitive Presence and improved Learning Outcomes. However, Peer Interaction and Technology Readiness did not directly influence Cognitive Engagement, indicating that technology familiarity and collaboration alone are not enough without effective learning support. Overall, these findings validate the expanded Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework and emphasize the importance of pedagogical design in integrating sustainable technology-based learning. This study contributes to the development of adaptive, technology-based, cognitively rich environments that support sustainable engineering education.

items.title: Factores organizacionales asociados al burnout en profesionales de salud, educación y telecomunicaciones: estudio cualitativo en la Baixada Fluminense, Brasil
items.abstract: The study identifies the organizational factors that contribute to the development of burnout syndrome among professionals in the health, education, and telecommunications sectors in the Baixada Fluminense region, part of the metropolitan area of the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. This is an exploratory study with a qualitative approach. Data was collected through semi-structured interviews with seven professionals, and the empirical material was analyzed following Bardin’s content analysis procedures. The results indicate that factors such as work overload, micromanagement, lack of autonomy, and a high-pressure environment are determinants of emotional exhaustion, reduced productivity, and high staff turnover. Participants identified work overload and the accumulation of duties, limited autonomy, pressure related to goals and deadlines, and insufficient organizational support as the main organizational factors. Several interviewees reported difficulties disconnecting from work, interference with their personal lives, fatigue, stress, and a perceived deterioration in emotional well-being. Some also reported having considered leaving their jobs. Most participants did not identify specific organizational actions aimed at preventing burnout, although one divergent experience involving institutional emotional health initiatives was observed. It is concluded that the absence of effective organizational strategies for burnout prevention perpetuates the vulnerability of these workers, reinforcing the urgent need for more localized and effective occupational health policies.

items.title: Foundations of Artificial Intelligence in Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technological innovations of the twenty-first century, fundamentally changing the way individuals learn, work, communicate, and solve complex problems. Although AI has become a prominent component of modern society only in recent decades, its conceptual foundations extend back several centuries through philosophical discussions concerning human intelligence, logical reasoning, and mechanical computation. The evolution of Artificial Intelligence represents a multidisciplinary journey involving computer science, mathematics, cognitive psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, philosophy, engineering, statistics, and data science. Continuous advancements in computational power, algorithmic development, data availability, and digital infrastructure have enabled AI to evolve from theoretical concepts into intelligent systems capable of performing tasks that traditionally required human intelligence. The earliest ideas related to artificial intelligence originated long before the invention of computers. Ancient civilizations imagined intelligent machines capable of mimicking human behaviour through myths, literature, and mechanical inventions. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, philosophers and mathematicians such as René Descartes, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, and George Boole contributed foundational concepts related to logic, reasoning, symbolic representation, and mathematical computation. Their work laid the intellectual groundwork for the development of computational systems capable of representing knowledge and making logical decisions.The modern evolution of Artificial Intelligence began during the twentieth century with the rapid advancement of computing technologies. In the 1930s and 1940s, significant progress in mathematical logic and computer science established the theoretical basis for intelligent machines. Alan Turing introduced the concept of a universal computing machine and later proposed the famous Turing Test, which examined whether a machine could demonstrate behaviour indistinguishable from that of a human being. Turing's pioneering contributions remain fundamental to contemporary AI research because they established that machines could potentially perform intelligent reasoning through computational processes. A major milestone occurred in 1956 during the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, organized by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, and Nathaniel Rochester. This conference formally introduced the term "Artificial Intelligence" and established AI as an independent scientific discipline. Researchers believed that human intelligence could be represented computationally and that machines could eventually perform reasoning, learning, language understanding, and problem-solving. The Dartmouth Conference inspired widespread academic interest and initiated decades of intensive research into intelligent computing systems.The period between the late 1950s and early 1970s is often referred to as the early development phase of Artificial Intelligence. During this era, researchers developed symbolic AI methods that emphasized logical reasoning, rule-based systems, theorem proving, and problem-solving algorithms. Early AI programmes successfully solved mathematical problems, played strategic games such as chess, and demonstrated limited natural language capabilities. Optimism surrounding AI research increased substantially as scientists believed that general human-level intelligence could be achieved within a relatively short period. However, limitations in computing power, data availability, memory capacity, and algorithmic efficiency restricted further progress. During the 1970s and 1980s, Artificial Intelligence experienced periods commonly known as the "AI Winters," characterized by reduced research funding, slower technological progress, and diminished public expectations. Many ambitious predictions regarding human-level machine intelligence proved unrealistic because available computing resources and algorithms were insufficient to support increasingly complex AI applications. Despite these challenges, important research continued in knowledge representation, expert systems, machine learning, robotics, and computational reasoning. Expert systems became particularly successful by capturing specialized human knowledge through rule-based decision-making frameworks that supported medical diagnosis, engineering design, financial analysis, and industrial management.The late 1980s and 1990s marked the gradual resurgence of Artificial Intelligence through the development of machine learning approaches. Rather than relying exclusively on manually programmed rules, researchers began designing algorithms capable of learning patterns directly from data. Statistical modelling, neural networks, evolutionary computation, fuzzy logic, probabilistic reasoning, and support vector machines expanded the capabilities of intelligent systems while improving adaptability, prediction accuracy, and decision-making performance. Significant improvements in computational hardware further accelerated AI research during this period. A landmark achievement occurred in 1997 when IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov, demonstrating the ability of intelligent computing systems to outperform human experts in highly specialized domains. This achievement attracted worldwide attention and illustrated the practical potential of Artificial Intelligence beyond theoretical research. Similar advances subsequently appeared in speech recognition, computer vision, autonomous robotics, medical diagnosis, financial forecasting, and industrial automation.The twenty-first century has witnessed unprecedented growth in Artificial Intelligence driven by three major technological developments: the availability of massive digital datasets, substantial improvements in computational processing power, and the emergence of advanced machine learning algorithms. The rapid expansion of the internet, cloud computing, mobile technologies, social media, and digital services generated enormous volumes of data that enabled intelligent systems to learn more effectively. Simultaneously, Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), high-performance computing, and cloud-based infrastructure significantly accelerated AI model training and deployment across diverse application domains. Deep learning has become one of the most influential developments in contemporary Artificial Intelligence. Inspired by the structure of the human brain, deep neural networks consist of multiple computational layers capable of learning complex representations from large datasets. These architectures have dramatically improved performance in image recognition, speech processing, language translation, autonomous driving, medical imaging, recommendation systems, fraud detection, and scientific research. Deep learning has transformed Artificial Intelligence from narrow task-specific applications into highly sophisticated systems capable of addressing increasingly complex real-world challenges.Natural Language Processing (NLP) has experienced remarkable advancement through transformer architectures and large language models capable of understanding, generating, summarizing, translating, and analysing human language with unprecedented accuracy. Conversational AI systems, intelligent virtual assistants, multilingual communication platforms, automated content generation, and research support tools have become integral components of education, healthcare, business, governance, and scientific research. These developments have substantially enhanced human-computer interaction while expanding opportunities for intelligent educational technologies. The emergence of generative Artificial Intelligence represents another significant milestone in AI evolution. Modern generative models can produce text, images, computer code, audio, video, simulations, educational content, and scientific documentation while supporting creativity, innovation, research, and personalized learning. These technologies have transformed knowledge creation and digital communication by enabling collaborative interactions between humans and intelligent systems across numerous professional disciplines.Artificial Intelligence has evolved beyond isolated computational applications into a foundational technology supporting digital transformation across multiple sectors. Healthcare employs AI for disease diagnosis, medical imaging, drug discovery, personalized treatment, and patient monitoring. Manufacturing integrates AI with robotics, predictive maintenance, quality control, and smart production systems. Financial institutions utilize intelligent algorithms for fraud detection, risk management, investment analysis, and customer services. Agriculture benefits from precision farming, crop monitoring, environmental analysis, and resource optimization. Transportation increasingly relies upon autonomous vehicles, intelligent traffic management, and logistics optimization. Education has emerged as one of the fastest-growing application areas where Artificial Intelligence supports personalized learning, intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, curriculum development, learning analytics, educational administration, and lifelong learning. items.title: From instructions to intelligent synthesis: conceptual art, distributed creativity, and the posthuman turn in AI-powered artistic practices
items.abstract: Abstract In recent years, the groundbreaking development of AI technologies such as text-to-image generation has revealed the unprecedented potential of machines in the realm of artistic creation. This has reignited and intensified widespread reflections on historical issues in artistic practice, including ontological questions, the identity of the author, the configuration of human–machine relationships, and the positioning of creativity. To address these concerns, this paper mainly seeks to draw inspiration from the important artistic thoughts of two conceptual artists who were active in the 1960s: Yoko Ono and Sol LeWitt. It also explores the interconnectedness and continuity between generative AI art practices and the legacy of conceptual art, tracing the historical trajectory of the relationship between conceptual art and digital art. Beyond the pivotal artistic practices of these two pioneering conceptual artists, the comparative analysis also encompasses the examination of additional associated artistic endeavors in relation to text-guided image synthesis. This broader scope of artists aims to more comprehensively support the argument on the impact of artificial intelligence on participatory frameworks and the concept of authorship within future creative practices. By delving into a discussion on dematerialization with conceptual art’s focus on concepts over material objects, the authors explore the potential for a posthumanist paradigm in AI art practices, to consider the reconfiguration of creativity in human–machine collaborations. Through speculative explorations of AI visualizations of Ono's and LeWitt's instructions and evaluating the role of "prompt engineering" in collaborative creation, new forms of distributed creativity that respond to posthumanist provocations are discovered. Leveraging the posthumanist emphasis on the “biological and microbiological entanglement with nonhumans”, this approach aids in dislodging the centrality of the individual or the artist within the creative process (Herbrechter 2023, p. 8). This critical examination highlights the disruptive potential of conceptual art in reshaping the notion of authorship within its symbiotic relationship with technological culture. It reveals the dynamic and co-evolutionary relationship between the conceptual art discourse and its reinterpretation within the emerging computational participatory structures of the artistic frontier. By drawing on the legacy of conceptual art, this study attempts to reconcile the tensions between conceptual completion, technological participation, artistic ontology, and distributed creativity, providing theoretical support for current AI art practices and driving the ongoing reconsideration of posthuman creative partnerships in technology mediated artistic production.

items.title: From Pilots to Production: Lessons in Cross-Institutional Federated Training and Artificial Intelligence for Science
items.abstract: Many of the most valuable scientific datasets cannot be centralized: they are proprietary, export-controlled, classified, or bound by data-sovereignty restrictions. This inverts the usual paradigm: the model must move to the data, making federated artificial intelligence (AI) core infrastructure for open science. We synthesize lessons from U.S. Department of Energy national laboratories, industry deployments, and the open-source community into a structured account of moving federated AI from pilot demonstrations to dependable, multi-site production. The lessons come from five concurrent efforts spanning leadership-class supercomputers and cloud infrastructure in regulated settings. We organize them around an adapted \textit{five-domain readiness frame} and a stratified view of the stack beneath a trained model: data architecture, privacy and security controls, trust and verification, governance and socio-technical factors, and operations, the layers that decide whether a pilot becomes dependable. The question shifts from ``can we train it?'' to ``can we operate it, audit it, and change it safely?'' We report systems lessons in memory efficiency, reliability, and synchronization; set out what privacy, security, and decentralized trust require in production, and what is not yet validated there; and identify cross-cutting open problems (asynchronous federation, leakage auditing, verification standards, and harmonized data contracts) that we argue warrant a dedicated, international, open-science working group.

items.title: From Ratings to Sensors: Real-Time AIIoT-Based Credibility Anchored on Blockchain for Ride-Sharing Ecosystems
items.abstract: Current ride-sharing platforms predominantly rely on subjective post-ride ratings to evaluate driver credibility, making reputation systems vulnerable to user bias, delayed feedback, collusion, and manipulation. Although recent studies have explored blockchain-based ride-sharing, AI-driven driver monitoring, and IoT-enabled transportation independently, they do not provide an integrated trust framework that continuously derives credibility from objectively verifiable driving behaviour while maintaining scalability and low operational cost.This paper presents Ridezy, a decentralized trust architecture that replaces conventional rating-based reputation with real-time sensor-driven credibility. The proposed framework combines edge Artificial Intelligence and Internet of Things (AIIoT) technologies to continuously monitor behavioural indicators such as lane discipline, speed compliance, braking behaviour, and traffic sign adherence. Instead of storing high-frequency telemetry on the blockchain, Ridezy employs a hybrid architecture in which behavioural summaries are processed off-chain and only cryptographic hashes, credibility updates, and payment records are anchored on Polygon smart contracts, enabling tamper-evident trust with minimal blockchain overhead. To evaluate the proposed architecture, Ridezy is compared against three representative trust models: a traditional rating-based system, an AI-only architecture, and a blockchain-only architecture. The evaluation considers behavioural detection performance, end-to-end latency, cost efficiency, throughput, reputation stability, tamper resistance, and component-wise ablation studies. Experimental results demonstrate that the hybrid architecture achieves higher behavioural fidelity and stronger trust guarantees than conventional reputation mechanisms while maintaining low per-ride blockchain cost and scalable operation through batched on-chain commitments.The primary contribution of this work is a sensor-driven credibility framework that transforms real-time behavioural evidence into a cryptographically verifiable trust primitive for ride-sharing ecosystems. By combining edge AI, IoT telemetry, and blockchain-based trust anchoring within a scalable hybrid architecture, Ridezy provides a practical foundation for trustworthy, transparent, and next-generation intelligent mobility systems.

items.title: From Structural Empowerment to Performance: A Sequential Mediation Model of Job-Design Empowerment, Psychological Empowerment, and Managerial Motivation among Bank Managers in a Developing Economy
items.abstract: Purpose: In an era of intense competition and rapid organizational change, perceived empowerment has become a critical lever for improving employee behavior and firm-level outcomes. This study examines how three empowerment approaches—perceived structural empowerment, perceived job design empowerment, and psychological empowerment—shape the task performance, contextual performance, and organizational commitment of middle-level managers in Pakistan's public and private commercial banks. Intrinsic motivation is modeled as a mediator and extrovert personality as a moderator of these relationships. Design/Methodology/Approach: Survey data were collected from 900 managers using convenience sampling, yielding 814 usable responses; data were analyzed with SPSS and AMOS using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling. Findings: Results show that perceived structural empowerment and perceived job design empowerment significantly and positively predict task performance, contextual performance, and organizational commitment, and that psychological empowerment partially mediates the effects of both forms of empowerment on these outcomes. Intrinsic motivation further mediates the relationship between psychological empowerment and the performance behaviors, while extrovert personality moderates the psychological empowerment–task performance and psychological empowerment–organizational commitment relationships but not the psychological empowerment–contextual performance relationship. Implications/Originality/Value: The findings offer banks an empowerment-based motivational framework for human resource policy that can strengthen employee performance and organizational commitment simultaneously.

items.title: Future Trends
items.abstract: AI is rapidly transforming the educational landscape, and its future impact is expected to extend beyond individual learning tools toward broader changes in teaching, assessment, institutional management, research, and educational ecosystems. Future developments may create increasingly intelligent and personalized learning environments in which humans and AI systems work together to support educational goals. The year 2035 represents an important horizon for considering the future development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education. By this period, AI may become deeply integrated into learning platforms, educational administration, research environments, assessment systems, digital classrooms, and professional education. The future of education is unlikely to be based on AI alone. Instead, educational environments may increasingly combine AI capabilities with human expertise, creativity, emotional intelligence, critical thinking, and ethical responsibility. A possible framework is: AI Technology + Human Expertise + Digital Infrastructure + Ethical Governance = Future Education By 2035, AI may become a regular component of educational environments rather than an additional technological tool. Students may interact with intelligent learning systems that continuously adapt to their learning progress, interests, abilities, and educational goals. Teachers may use AI to support lesson planning, assessment, learning analytics, content development, and personalized instruction.

items.title: GENERATIVE AI ADOPTION BY SMES: DRIVERS, BARRIERS AND PERFORMANCE OUTCOMES IN NIGERIA
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is creating new opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to improve business processes, innovation, productivity, and competitiveness. However, the factors encouraging or limiting Generative AI adoption and its performance outcomes among SMEs in Nigeria remain underexplored. This study examines Generative AI adoption by SMEs in Nigeria, focusing on its drivers, barriers, and performance outcomes. A cross-sectional survey research design was employed, with data collected from 200 SME owners, managers, and employees using a structured questionnaire titled Generative AI Adoption and SME Performance Questionnaire (GAIA-SPQ), validated with a reliability coefficient of 0.86. Data were analyzed using correlation analysis at a 0.05 level of significance. Findings reveal that drivers of Generative AI significantly influence its adoption, while barriers also significantly affect adoption negatively. The study further finds that Generative AI use significantly affects SME performance, particularly in relation to productivity and innovation. The study concludes that Generative AI provides important opportunities for improving SME performance, although effective adoption requires favourable conditions and the reduction of implementation barriers. It is recommended that SMEs strengthen their technological capabilities, develop relevant digital skills, and adopt cost-effective Generative AI solutions to improve productivity, innovation, and competitiveness.

items.title: Generative AI in Islamic Education: A Maqāṣid-Based Framework for Curriculum, Assessment and Academic Integrity
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered Islamic schools, seminaries and universities faster than the institutions can govern it. Students use chatbots to explain verses, draft essays and prepare for examinations, while teachers lack shared rules on what is permitted, how to disclose it and how to assess learning fairly. This paper proposes a practical framework that grounds those decisions in the objectives of the Sharia (maqāṣid al-sharīʿa) rather than in generic ethics alone. Using an analytical synthesis of recent evidence on generative AI in education, research on assessment and academic integrity, international governance guidance, and the maqāṣid literature, the paper maps the five classical necessities (religion, life, intellect, lineage and property) onto the risks of AI-mediated learning and derives design principles for three layers: curriculum, assessment and academic integrity. The framework calls for AI literacy grounded in the ethic of verification, assessment built on authentic and oral demonstration of understanding instead of unreliable detection software, a three-tier policy on permitted use with disclosure, and governance that protects learner data and religious content. A phased implementation route and indicators are offered for institutions. The paper is conceptual and untested in practice; it closes with a research agenda for piloting the framework, comparing it across legal schools and measuring its effects on learning.

items.title: Generative AI-Assisted Competitive Microlearning Strategy: Development and Validation of the Plomp Model in Classroom Teacher Education in Finland
items.abstract: Background. The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education has created challenges in designing responsible and adaptive learning strategies. Meanwhile, competitive elements in gamified learning remain debated due to inconsistent effects on learner engagement. Purpose. This research aimed to develop and evaluate a generative AI-assisted competitive microlearning strategy for improving instructional media development skills among Finnish Luokanopettajakoulutus (Class Teacher Education) students. Novelty. This study introduces a novel instructional design that integrates generative AI, microlearning, and optional quality-based competition. Unlike conventional competitive gamification approaches, the proposed strategy recognizes learner differences by examining whether competition produces varied outcomes across learning groups Method. Using the Plomp development model, the study involved 79 undergraduate students from four parallel classes. Data from expert validation, practicality questionnaires, and product assessments were analyzed using Aiken’s V and descriptive statistics. Results. The strategy achieved high validity (Aiken’s V = 0.87) and strong practicality (83.1% student response; 85.9% lecturer response). Variation in competition participation (41–62%) indicated different effects among learner groups. Conclusion. The findings contribute an adaptive AI-assisted microlearning framework that balances innovation, learner diversity, and educational equity in teacher education.

items.title: H-VALIDA: A Hybrid Methodological Framework for Transparent AI-Assisted Surveys in Data-Scarce Contexts: A Conceptual Framework for Responsible AI Integration
items.abstract: Survey research has taken up artificial intelligence quickly, largely because of speed, scale, and lower cost. Those same gains bring methodological risks that become especially serious where data are thin, several languages are in use, or cultural meaning is tightly layered. This article puts forward H-VALIDA (Hybrid Validation and Auditing for Localized, Interpretable, Documented, and Accountable AI-Assisted Surveys) as both a conceptual and an operational framework for AI-assisted surveys that are more reliable, more sensitive to context, and more firmly grounded in ethics. The framework draws together critical data studies, human-centred AI, the total survey error tradition, classical survey methodology, and decolonial principles of data governance. Seven interlocking pillars organise the work: Hybrid Human-AI Collaboration, Contextual Sampling, Algorithmic Auditing, Human Validation, Source Triangulation, Open Documentation, and Ethical Accountability. Those pillars are mapped onto an expanded total survey error taxonomy, and the CARE Principles for Indigenous data governance run through the design as a whole. The article is a methodological design study rather than a field experiment. Development of the framework followed a five-stage protocol: a diagnostic review of documented weaknesses in AI-assisted surveys; a structured synthesis of the literature; integration of principles; construction of the pillars; and operationalisation. Prospective appraisal rested on a specified heuristic rubric, a worked multilingual scenario, and a comparison with a purely automated baseline. No expert-panel scores, statistical tests, or national field implementation are reported here. Claims of improvement are therefore stated as theoretically grounded and operationally specified propositions that still require empirical confirmation. The central argument is that AI systems function as sociotechnical arrangements rather than as neutral instruments, and that validity depends on continuous human oversight, an open record of process, and deliberate adjustment to local conditions.

items.title: How Artificial Intelligence Shapes Human Narratives
items.abstract: How can artificial intelligence (AI) best support human problem-solving, creativity, and group work? I introduce a psychological account of narrative agency that formalizes how human groups learn from, communicate, and influence narratives in digital contexts. I then discuss how AI models impact human performance through a narrative agency lens, from authoring better essays to finding consensus online. Crucially, AI outputs are routed through a human's narrative agency to generate a result that causes change in the world. Designing human–AI systems around maintaining people's narrative agency is therefore essential for human–AI alignment.

items.title: How Bridging and Bonding Social Capital Shapes Performance Expectancy of Digital Transformation Among Immigrants and Natives
items.abstract: Performance expectancy, individuals’ beliefs about the usefulness of digital transformation, could impact individuals’ intention, use, and satisfaction with technologies, yet remains an understudied topic among immigrant populations. Drawing on social capital theory, we examine how bonding and bridging social capital shape performance expectancy across different domains of digital transformation and whether these associations differ by nativity status. Using the 2022 Digital Divide Survey (N = 8,400; 7,000 native South Koreans, 700 marriage immigrants, 700 North Korean migrants), regression analyses showed that bridging social capital had positive associations with performance expectancy (b ranging from 0.43 to 0.62, p < 0.001), whereas bonding social capital was negative, particularly for networking (b = −0.09, p < 0.001) and remote work/learning (b = −0.08, p < 0.001). North Korean migrants reported the highest adjusted means of performance expectancy across all domains. Results highlight that diverse social networks generate greater perceived benefits from digital transformation.

items.title: How do humans infer silent reliability degradation in automated decision aids? A computational modelling study of first failure reports
items.abstract: Automated decision aids may undergo silent reliability degradation, in which performance declines without explicit warnings, confidence cues, or reliability-state feedback. In such situations, humans must infer whether automation has degraded from sequences of correct and incorrect outputs. This study examined the computational mechanisms underlying first failure reports in an industrial visual inspection task. We conceptualized silent-failure perception as a training-baseline-referenced first-report problem and compared five candidate mechanisms within a shared discrete-time hazard framework: Bayesian reliability learning, Delta-rule learning, CUSUM cumulative-deviation inference, recent-window heuristic monitoring, and a no-learning/reporting-tendency baseline. Trial-level data from 60 participants were analysed across three levels of failure severity and two levels of initial reliability, yielding 720 participant-scenario observations with first-report times or right-censored outcomes. PSIS-LOO model comparison showed that the Delta-rule learning model provided the strongest predictive account overall and across all reliability conditions. Posterior predictive checks further indicated that this model reproduced the cumulative time course of first failure reports. The results suggest that humans infer silent reliability degradation by tracking a current error-state estimate relative to the training baseline: errors increase this estimate, correct feedback suppresses it, and first reports become more likely when the current state shows sufficient baseline-relative deviation. Failure severity primarily shaped the density and persistence of degradation evidence, whereas initial reliability shaped the experiential baseline against which later errors were interpreted. These findings provide a mechanistic account of silent-failure perception and inform the design of reliability-transparent automated systems.

items.title: How do virtual exercise technology and social presence influence motivation to exercise?
items.abstract: Introduction Virtual technology offers a promising tool for encouraging engagement in exercise, as it can provide the user with enhanced visual stimuli and accessible metrics; however, the specific features within that technology that contribute to motivation and participation require further investigation. This study examined how different visual displays and the presence of a second rider influenced motivation to exercise using virtual technology. Methods Twenty-four young adults completed a 3-km cycling course on the same virtual track under three counterbalanced conditions including (a) a metrics-only ride, where a screen in front of the rider displayed only standard performance variables (e.g., power, cadence), (b) a solo-virtual ride, which was identical to the previous condition, but with the addition of the participant being depicted on the screen as an avatar amongst virtual scenery, and (c) a paired-virtual ride, that contained the same elements as the previous two conditions, but with the addition of a second rider represented on the screen as an avatar. Results The quantitative results, which included performance-related variables (cadence, power, speed, and heart rate), measures of intrinsic motivation, and ratings of perceived exertion, revealed significantly higher values for the paired-virtual condition compared to both the metrics-only and the solo-virtual conditions. Differences between the metrics-only and the solo-virtual conditions were isolated to interest-enjoyment and effort-importance. Brief interviews with participants indicated that the paired-virtual condition produced heightened levels of enjoyment and competitive drive which motivated participants to exert more effort. The solo-virtual condition was reported to be relaxing, but it was also reported as the least engaging. The metrics-only condition provoked negative emotions due to the absence of distractions and a heightened focus on internal cues. Discussion The results highlight the psychological mechanisms that influence motivation and engagement when using virtual exercise technology.

items.title: How, Not How Much? Exploring Help-Seeking Orientation and Academic Engagement in Student AI Use
items.abstract: Research often operationalizes AI use in terms of frequency; however, frequency alone does not capture why or how students use AI. Drawing on help-seeking theory, we examined whether instrumental (learning-oriented) versus executive (task-completion) orientation toward AI differentiates students in ways that frequency does not, using a survey of 107 undergraduates. Academic self-efficacy mediated the academic engagement-AI literacy association, with cognitive engagement showing the strongest engagement-literacy link. AI use frequency was negatively associated with academic engagement; this relationship remained negative and was larger in magnitude when controlling for AI literacy. Instrumental users showed higher academic engagement than executive users, despite no difference in usage frequency. These findings suggest that whether AI is treated as a thinking partner or an answer source may be more meaningful than exposure frequency alone. Implications are discussed for how educators and course designers assess and support learning-oriented AI use, including distance and online learning contexts, where self-regulated AI use is particularly consequential.

items.title: Human Factor Contributions to Accidents and Fatalities in U.S. Construction: A Comparative Analysis of Three Major Subsectors
items.abstract: Human factors remain a leading cause of occupational accidents and fatalities in the construction industry. Although human factors are a major contributor to construction accidents, their relative impact across different construction subsectors has not been fully quantified. This study presents a comparative analysis of accident and fatality data from the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) for three major construction subsectors, NAICS 236 (Construction of Buildings), 237 (Heavy and Civil Engineering Construction), and 238 (Specialty Trade Contractors) from January 2010 through June 2025. Seventy human-factor-related keywords were categorized into eight categories, and accident counts, fatality counts, and fatality rates, defined as the proportion of investigated cases that were fatal, were computed. Twenty-four high-frequency keywords (≥60 investigated accidents) were further analyzed across the three subsectors. Descriptive methods, including risk matrices, Pareto analysis, and category-level fatality rate comparisons, were applied to identify the factors contributing most to fatalities. Differences between subsectors were tested using permutation-based chi-square tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Results indicate substantial variation in both frequency and severity among keywords. At the category level, cognitive or perceptual errors, procedural violations and unsafe acts, and judgment and awareness failures in equipment use showed significantly higher fatality proportions in Heavy and Civil Engineering Construction than in the other two subsectors, whereas at the keyword level only lost balance and inattention differed significantly once the correction was applied. The findings provide a data-driven basis for prioritizing targeted safety interventions and tailoring human factor mitigation strategies to subsector-specific risks.
